title: Rename etymon.synset_id → etymon.cognate_id (lexicon schema cleanup)
description:
Pre-existing concern flagged during PR #61 review (Claude M1): the etymon.synset_id column populated by cluster-cognates is misnamed. It represents a COGNATE-cluster ID (etymology-based: OE tūn / ON tún / Icelandic tún all share one cluster pointing at PGmc *tūnaz). The new wyrd-7tz Phase 1 introduced the meaning_synset table (semantic equivalence), creating a naming collision that's documented in lexicon.sql but is fragile.

The right rename:
- etymon.synset_id → etymon.cognate_id
- etymon.synset_method → etymon.cognate_method
- idx_etymon_synset → idx_etymon_cognate

Touchpoints (callsites in lexicon.py + cli.py):
- cluster_cognates() and its tests
- migrate_schema migration entries
- Any reports / stats command that reads synset_id

Should land before wyrd-7tz Phase 2 ships (LLM-assisted etymon_meaning_synset population) so future code only ever sees the disambiguated naming.

Out of scope for wyrd-7tz Phase 1 — kept as a separate cleanup to keep that PR's scope tight.

title: Generator.filter_for_tag: sort set iteration to lock cross-PYTHONHASHSEED bit-stability
description:
Pre-existing concern flagged during PR #59 review (Claude + seed-reproducibility-reviewer): wyrd/generators/kenning/proportions.py:filter_for_tag builds a dict by iterating a set comprehension over tag_db keys. The resulting dict's iteration order then feeds weighted_choice via Generator.select, where the cumulative-threshold construction is order-dependent.

Within one process the order is stable (PYTHONHASHSEED is fixed at startup). Across processes with different PYTHONHASHSEED, the dict iteration order can vary, which can flip weighted_choice picks at boundaries.

Same root cause as the wyrd-mj2 fix in _raw_class_score (PR #59); same fix shape applies — sort the iteration before building the dict.

Suggested change:
    keys_set = set(keys)
    return {key: self.elements[key] for key in sorted(keys_set) if key in self.elements}

Add a regression test analogous to test_raw_class_score_is_bit_stable_across_python_hash_seed: subprocess loop with varied PYTHONHASHSEED, assert weighted_choice returns the same key across runs.

Pre-existing — not introduced by PR #59. Was deliberately not bundled into PR #59 to keep scope tight.
close_reason: Closed

title: kenning: move default lexicon DB location to ~/.wyrd/lexicon.db
description:
Currently _DEFAULT_LEXICON_PATH in cli.py is cwd-relative ('wyrd/generators/kenning/data/lexicon.db'). This is fragile in worktree workflows: a 'wyrd kenning lexicon build' run from a worktree's cwd silently creates a divergent DB in that worktree's data/ dir.

Move the default to '~/.wyrd/lexicon.db' (with WYRD_LEXICON_DB env override) so the location is independent of cwd / repo / worktree. One DB per user, survives 'rm -rf' of any checkout, fresh clones inherit the existing corpus.

Scope:

1. Add wyrd.generators.kenning.paths module (or similar) with default_lexicon_path() that returns Path.home() / '.wyrd' / 'lexicon.db', overridable via WYRD_LEXICON_DB env var.
2. Update _DEFAULT_LEXICON_PATH in cli.py to call this function.
3. Auto-migrate: on first command that needs the DB, if the new path doesn't exist AND a legacy path 'wyrd/generators/kenning/data/lexicon.db' exists relative to the git repo root, mv the file with a stderr warning. Don't auto-create ~/.wyrd unless we're committing to using it.
4. Add 'wyrd kenning lexicon path' CLI command that prints the resolved DB path (operator convenience).
5. Update OVERVIEW.md and INGESTION.md references to the new default location.
6. Drop the 'wyrd/generators/kenning/data/lexicon.db' line from .gitignore (no longer needed since the file won't exist there).
7. Tests: cover default-path resolution, env override, auto-migration of legacy DB.

Acceptance:
- _DEFAULT_LEXICON_PATH resolves cwd-independently
- 'wyrd kenning lexicon path' prints the right path
- Legacy DB at wyrd/generators/kenning/data/lexicon.db migrates to ~/.wyrd/lexicon.db on first command run with stderr warning

title: bridge_phonological_oe: fix target-index to follow merged_into_id chains + expand bridge table
description:
Diagnostic on 2026-05-03 (post wyrd-083/ft3 merge): OE residue is 1510 unbridged of 1830 unmerged OE place-name etymons.

Two issues identified:

ISSUE A: bridge_phonological_oe target_index bug.
The target_index is built with 'WHERE merged_into_id IS NULL', so when the bridge map names a target that is itself a tombstone, the lookup fails silently.

Concrete failures from current DB state:
- 'dale' → 'dæl': dæl is merged into dael (id 1426). Lookup misses. (5 sources unbridged)
- 'ey' → 'īeg': īeg doesn't exist as canonical at all (only 'ieg' does, macron-stripped). Lookup misses. (5 sources unbridged)

Fix: when building target_index, follow merged_into_id chains so target lookup resolves through tombstones to the live canonical. Or alternatively, snap bridge values to the actual canonical-form spelling per current DB state — but the redirect-follow fix is more robust against future ingest re-shuffles.

ISSUE B: _OE_PHONOLOGICAL_BRIDGES is too narrow.
Top high-witness OE forms still unbridged after wyrd-ft3 (sources count in parens):
  ingas (7), wella (4), scelf (3), holegn (3), inga (3), hare (3), wlc (3),
  cippa (3), hang (3), pool (3), leofhere (3), lech (3), hasel (3), cylla (3),
  kirk (3), writol (2), hala (2), hīgna (2), kers (2), draeg (2), roth (2),
  ticce (2), hāran (2), hēg (2), cloppa (2), billing (2), ēg (2), hlyp (2)
... and ~50 more 2-source forms.

Add the high-witness pairs to _OE_PHONOLOGICAL_BRIDGES. Each has a known Wiktionary canonical (often macroned: ingas → ingas/-ingas, wella → welle/wiella, holegn → holen, hare → hara, pool → pōl, kirk → cirice, etc.). Cross-reference each addition against actual DB state via a quick SELECT.

- Issue B: bridge table expanded by 30-50 high-witness pairs sourced from current DB

title: D5-1 expansion: extend lookup-attested-years to also scan toponym_etymology rows
description:
Follow-up to wyrd-3ux (PR #47). The v1 lookup-attested-years scans etymon_text_match rows — those are reverse-search hits where canonical etymon forms appear in source bodies. Yield: 136 attestations on 5,298 rows (~2.6% density), well below the wyrd-3ux aspirational 1000+ target.

The reason for low density: reverse-search rows are MENTIONS of forms in scholarly prose, not necessarily citations. Real toponym citations with year-attestations live in toponym_etymology.notes — the LLM-extracted snippet that surrounded each toponym's body in the source dictionary.

Sample toponym_etymology notes: 'Kerorven, manoir en Guérande, 1476' or 'Tune, 1086 (DB); Tunes, 1242'. These have YEAR CITATIONS DIRECTLY in the captured snippet. Per a quick sample, ~40-60% of notes rows contain year citations.

Scope:

1. Schema: add attested_year column to toponym_etymology (or to toponym_etymology_element if attestations are per-element). Decide based on whether the LLM extracts per-element years or just one per toponym.
2. Function: lookup_attested_years_for_etymologies(db) — scans toponym_etymology.notes (no source bodies needed; the quote is in-DB). Apply the same form-attached pattern.
3. CLI: extend lookup-attested-years to also process toponym_etymology rows when present.
4. Tests: parametrize over both etymon_text_match and toponym_etymology shapes.

Estimated yield: corpus has ~5,238 toponym_etymology rows. At 30-40% density (year-citations are common in toponym dictionary entries), expected new attestations: 1,500-2,000.

Acceptance:
- Combined etymon_text_match + toponym_etymology yield >= 1,000 (per wyrd-3ux original target)
- FP rate stays <= 5% (form-attached pattern is the same)
- Reversible via clear-enrichment --stage=attested-years (works on both tables)

title: cluster-cognates / lexicon: bridge generic 'celtic' language code to specific Welsh/Irish/Gaelic/Breton entries
description:
Discovered during 2026-05-03 wiktextract ingest: 441 place-name dictionary etymons with language='celtic' have no synset cluster despite their forms (ar, ach, dubh, ros, caer, fionn, cill, druim, ...) being well-attested in Wiktionary under specific Celtic language codes (cy=Welsh, ga=Irish, gd=Scottish Gaelic, br=Breton, gv=Manx, kw=Cornish, sga=Old Irish, cel-pro=Proto-Celtic).

Place-name dictionaries don't pin which specific Celtic language a morpheme is from — they write 'celtic' as a catch-all. Wiktionary entries are language-specific. The lookup mismatch leaves a real cross-source bridge unbuilt.

Fix options:

(A) New normalize-celtic CLI / lib pass: for each etymon with language='celtic', search for matching canonical_form in {welsh, irish, scottish-gaelic, breton, manx, cornish, proto-celtic} and merge via merged_into_id (D22 OCR-cluster style — non-destructive). The Celtic etymon becomes a tombstone pointing at whichever specific-language match exists. Cluster-cognates then rolls up via the merged_into_id chain (already redirect-aware per wyrd-223).

(B) Multi-language fuzzy search in cluster-cognates: when finding edges, treat 'celtic' as a wildcard that matches any of the specific Celtic language codes. More invasive; option A is cleaner.

Acceptance: post-implementation, the Celtic place-name etymons (ros, caer, dubh, fionn, etc.) appear in clusters with their Wiktionary specific-language counterparts. Coverage of place-name etymons with synset_id rises from 17.6%.

Out of scope: phonological-similarity matching (ton vs tūn vowel-weakening) — separate ticket.
close_reason: Closed

title: wiktextract descendants section: parse nested tree shape (not flat-with-depth)
description:
Discovered during PR #41 live ingest 2026-05-03: wiktextract's actual descendants shape is a NESTED tree, not the flat-with-depth-markers list my parser assumed. Each descendant entry has {lang_code, word, optional descendants (recursive)} — there is NO 'templates' field on descendant entries and NO 'depth' field.

Concrete real entry from sources/wiktextract_proto_celtic.jsonl:
  {'lang': 'Proto-Brythonic', 'lang_code': 'cel-bry-pro', 'word': '*ɨn', 'descendants': [{'lang': 'Middle Breton', 'lang_code': 'xbm', 'word': 'en', 'descendants': [...]}]}

Result: the OE slice ingest yielded 0 downward edges across 66179 entries because the parser walked a non-existent 'templates' field. All useful descent edges came from the etymology UPWARD direction instead. That's still ~10K edges but loses the downward tree (parents whose descendants we don't have entries for).

Fix: rewrite _walk_descendants in wyrd/generators/kenning/wiktextract_ingester.py to:
- Read lang_code + word directly from each descendants entry (not via templates)
- Recurse into the nested 'descendants' field on each entry (true tree walk)
- Drop the depth-markers logic entirely (replaced by recursion depth)
- Handle borrow flag if present in the new shape (need to investigate — may be on 'tags' or 'roman' fields)

Tests: need a fresh fixture matching the real nested shape. The existing tests use the wrong (flat-with-depth) shape and would need to be either deleted or kept as 'historical-fixture-style' tests with a comment.

Synthetic test data should be built from a small slice of real wiktextract output (e.g. 5-10 lines from sources/wiktextract_proto_celtic.jsonl) committed as a test fixture under tests/fixtures/.

Acceptance criteria:
- _walk_descendants reads {lang_code, word, descendants?} directly
- Recursive descent through nested 'descendants' arrays
- Test fixture from real wiktextract output (small, deterministic)
- Live ingest of sources/wiktextract_proto_celtic.jsonl (1608 entries, dense descendants) yields significant downward_edges count (currently 0)

title: cluster-cognates: walk through merged_into_id redirects to land synset_id on canonical winners
description:
Discovered during the wyrd-hun (PR #41) live ingest 2026-05-03: the cluster-cognates pass operates on RAW etymon_descent edges and assigns synset_id to whichever endpoint the edge points at — including OCR-merged tombstones.

Concrete case: wiktextract has OE 'tun' (ASCII), place-name dictionaries have OE 'tūn' (macron). normalize-ocr correctly merges them ('tun' becomes a tombstone with merged_into_id pointing at 'tūn'). But the wiktextract descent edge (gmw-pro:*tūn → ang:tun) still points at the tombstoned 'tun' (id=2274), not the canonical 'tūn' (id=716). cluster-cognates then assigns synset_id on the tombstone, leaving canonical 'tūn' with synset_id=NULL.

Result: queries like 'cognates of OE tūn' return empty because they look up synset_id on the canonical row. The rollup-aware query exists but is gnarly (walk merged_into_id chain to find loser, get synset_id from loser, find other rows with same synset_id, roll those through merged_into_id again).

Fix options:

(A) cluster-cognates walks etymon_canonical (the view that filters out merged_into_id IS NOT NULL) and resolves edges through merged_into_id → canonical. Writes synset_id on canonicals only. Tombstones rolled up at query time.

(B) After OCR merge, rewrite etymon_descent.parent_id and child_id to point at canonical winners. Mining-evidence-preserving since the edge metadata stays. But mutating the descent table feels like a D21 violation (mining evidence is sacred).

Option A is correct per D22 ('enrichment passes operate on canonical view; tombstones are queried-through, not mutated').

Acceptance criteria:
- cluster-cognates resolves parent_id and child_id through merged_into_id when finding roots and walking children
- After PR #41's OE ingest + normalize-ocr, query for synset_id of canonical OE 'tūn' (id=716) returns the *tūn cluster's id
- existing wyrd-81n tests still pass (the merged_into_id paths weren't exercised; new tests add coverage)
- regression test: insert raw edges A→B, then merge B into B' via OCR, then run cluster-cognates → synset_id lands on B' not on B (the tombstone)
close_reason: Shipped in PR #44

title: wyrd-4rt.1: wiktextract → etymon_descent ingester (Claude 1 implementation)
description:
Per user 2026-05-03: Wiktionary mining moves to Claude 1's lane (claude 2 stays on place-name etymology mining). Wiktextract is a pure structured-data ingester — no LLM, no form-in-body validation — so it doesn't fit claude 2's mine-llm pipeline shape.

Scope (this ticket):

(1) Library: parse wiktextract JSONL (one entry per line), extract:
    - word + lang_code → upsert etymon
    - etymology_templates: {{inh|...}} → inheritance edge upward, {{bor|...}} → borrowing, {{der|...}} → derivation, {{cal|...}} → calque
    - descendants section: each {{desc|<lang>|<word>}} → inheritance edge downward (Wiktionary defaults Descendants to inheritance unless explicitly flagged)
    - skip: {{cog|...}} (peer relation, no parent direction → optional 'cognate' edge if both in DB), {{m|...}} (mention only), pronunciation/qualifier/sense templates
    - depth field in descendants tracks nesting; sub-descendants chain off their nearest preceding entry at depth-1

(2) Lang code mapping: wiktextract uses Wiktionary lang codes (ang, gem-pro, non, is, en, de, ...) which differ from wyrd's existing language strings (old-english, proto-germanic, old-norse, icelandic, modern-english, german, ...). Build a lookup table for the ~30 codes we'll encounter most often; unmapped codes pass through raw with a counter.

(3) CLI: wyrd kenning lexicon ingest-wiktionary <path> with --apply / --db / --limit <N> / --since-line <N> for resumability.

(4) Source attribution: one synthetic source row 'wiktionary' (per D27).

(5) Idempotency: edge insertion is INSERT OR IGNORE on the (parent_id, child_id, edge_type, source_id) UNIQUE constraint; etymon upsert handles duplicates. Re-running on the same JSONL is a no-op.

(6) Tests: synthetic JSONL fixtures covering canonical entry shape, each edge-type template, descendants nesting, lang-code mapping, idempotency, malformed-entry skipping.

(7) Documentation: INGESTION.md gets a new 'Wiktionary mining (wyrd-4rt)' section with the kaikki.org dump URLs, slice strategies (per-language vs full corpus), and the ingest CLI.

Out of scope:
- Actually downloading the multi-GB wiktextract dump in a session — defer; user runs the dump pull manually and points the CLI at it.
- Compound/affix template handling (defer; the bulk of useful data is in inh/bor/der/cal/desc templates).
- Per-edit Wiktionary attribution (single 'wiktionary' source for v1 per D27).
- Cluster-cognates run after ingestion (already shipped wyrd-81n; user runs 'wyrd kenning lexicon cluster-cognates --apply' as a follow-up).

Acceptance criteria:
- New module wyrd/generators/kenning/wiktextract_ingester.py
- CLI 'wyrd kenning lexicon ingest-wiktionary' with --apply default-False (dry-run) flag

title: cluster-cognates enrichment pass: walk etymon_descent to populate synset_id
description:
Why this exists:

Once etymon_descent (filed as a sibling design ticket) lands and Wiktionary ingestion (wyrd-4rt) populates edges, we need a pass that walks the descent graph and assigns synset_id to every etymon reachable from a common root. Same shape as link-lemmas (D8): conservative, reversible, method-stamped.

Without this, queries like 'all cognates of Modern English town across languages' require an unbounded recursive CTE on every call. The materialized synset_id column makes it a single JOIN.

What needs to be done:

(1) New CLI: 'wyrd kenning lexicon cluster-cognates --apply'
    - Walks etymon_descent edges of edge_type IN ('inheritance', 'borrowing') from the most-ancestral etymons (those with no incoming descent edges of these types)
    - Assigns synset_id = id of the root to every descendant
    - Skips the 'cognate' edge_type (that's a 'compare with' relationship, not a chain)
    - Method/version stamp: etymon.synset_method = 'cluster-cognates-v1'

(2) Reversibility: 'wyrd kenning lexicon clear-enrichment --stage=cognates --apply' clears synset_id and synset_method. Reuses the existing clear-enrichment shape from D22.

(3) Tests:
    - A → B → C inheritance chain: all three get the same synset_id (= A.id)
    - Multi-root case: separate roots produce separate synset_ids
    - Cognate edges (edge_type='cognate') do NOT bridge synsets — cognate is a peer relationship, not a chain
    - Clear + re-run is a no-op (idempotent)
    - Borrowing edges DO bridge (we treat borrowed words as part of the cognate set; refine if this turns out to be too permissive)

Acceptance criteria:
- CLI command exists and is documented in INGESTION.md
- Tests as above
- Clear-enrichment knows about --stage=cognates

title: Design etymon_descent schema + cognate-cluster query layer for cross-language reflex graph
description:
Why this exists:

Wiktionary etymology + Descendants sections produce a directed graph that doesn't fit the current schema. A Proto-Germanic root like *tūnaz has children in OE (tūn), ON (tún), modern Icelandic (tún), Faroese (tún), modern English (town), German (Zaun), Dutch (tuin). The current etymon table has merged_into_id (OCR-cluster losers, D22) and lemma_id (inflected variants of the same form, D8) — neither represents 'this OE form descends from this Proto-Germanic form' or 'this Icelandic word is a cognate of this English word.'

Without this schema, we can't:
- Mine Wiktermextract output (wyrd-4rt) without losing the chain information
- Surface 'modern descendants of OE tūn' as a query
- Render a place name in a different language register by swapping each etymon for its Welsh/Icelandic/Latin cognate (the cross-cultural rendering use case)
- Implement wyrd-7tz (synset / cross-language equivalence) — the Descendants tree IS the synset

Scope (this ticket):

Schema design + DECISIONS.md entry. NOT the actual ingestion (that's wyrd-4rt) and NOT the cognate-clustering enrichment pass (separate follow-on ticket). This ticket lands the tables and the query examples; wyrd-4rt populates them.

Key design decisions to record:

(1) Edge table shape — proposed:
    CREATE TABLE etymon_descent (
      id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
      parent_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etymon(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
      child_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etymon(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
      edge_type TEXT NOT NULL,  -- 'inheritance'|'borrowing'|'calque'|'compound'|'derivation'|'cognate'|'unknown'
      source_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES source(id),
      confidence TEXT CHECK (confidence IN ('high','medium','low')),
      notes TEXT,
      UNIQUE (parent_id, child_id, edge_type, source_id)
    );
    Plus indexes on parent_id, child_id.

(2) Edge types map to Wiktextract template kinds: {{inh}}=inheritance (high conf), {{bor}}=borrowing (high), {{cog}}=cognate-relation (medium), {{der}}=derivation (medium), free-text 'compare with X'=low. Document the mapping in INGESTION.md once wyrd-4rt lands.

(3) Should descent edges contribute to etymon_consensus.witnesses? PROPOSED: no. Descent ≠ extraction-attestation (D4 is about 'N scholars cite this morpheme as part of a toponym's breakdown'). Descent rolls up cross-language and would inflate consensus counts. Synset clustering is the right rollup for descent.

(4) Synset / cognate cluster layer — proposed: materialized via etymon.synset_id (nullable INTEGER), populated by a separate 'wyrd kenning lexicon cluster-cognates' pass that walks the descent graph from each Proto-* root and assigns synset_id to all reachable descendants. Same shape as link-lemmas (D8) — derivable, reversible, method-stamped via etymon.synset_method.
   Alternative considered: recursive CTE view. Rejected because cross-language synset queries would walk unbounded depth on every call; materialized column makes the query a single JOIN.

(5) Wiktionary as source: one synthetic 'wiktionary' source row for v1 (per-edit attribution lives in wiki history; per-language-section slicing is overkill until needed).

(6) Generality: the schema accepts descent edges from ANY source, not just Wiktionary. Existing dictionary mining that says 'from OE tūn' could populate descent rows too — just hasn't been the focus. Generalize the schema; let wyrd-4rt be the first big populator.

Acceptance criteria:
- New D-entry in DECISIONS.md (D27?) documenting (1)-(6) with rationale
- Schema changes in data/lexicon.sql + migration in lexicon.py
- Sample queries in INGESTION.md or a new section: 'modern descendants of <etymon>', 'cognates of <etymon>', 'languages with a reflex meaning <gloss>'
- Tests cover: schema migration is idempotent; insert/query round-trips; etymon_consensus does NOT roll up across descent edges
- wyrd-4rt updated to depend on this ticket
- New ticket filed for the cluster-cognates enrichment pass (synset_id populator), depending on this ticket

Out of scope:
- Actual Wiktionary ingestion (wyrd-4rt)
- Cluster-cognates enrichment pass (new follow-on ticket)
- Generator-side use of the descent/synset layer (e.g. cross-cultural rendering) — that's a third follow-on

title: Chrestomathy/treatise-aware extractor: pull only etymology-commentary sections from non-dictionary sources
description:
Pattern surfaced from 4 mining attempts (Watson 1904, Quilgars 1906, Longnon 1920 vol 2, Loth 1890): the existing alphabetical-headword parser is mis-matched for treatises, chrestomathies, and methodological essays. Real etymology content is BURIED inside chapter prose or commentary sections, but the parser segments by capital-letter headwords and treats each as a candidate entry — so the LLM sees front-matter / TOC / text excerpts / numbered-list section-headers and correctly declines them.

Concrete failure shapes seen at mining time:
1. Longnon vol 2 saint-names: 2,775 parser entries, 2% accept on first 50 because front-matter dominates. The actual saint-name body is a numbered list ('1725. Euphrasia: Sainte-Euphrasie ...') that the headword parser can't break out into per-saint rows.
2. Loth 1890 Chrestomathie: 615 entries, mostly Middle Breton text excerpts (mystery plays, prose). The dense etymology commentary I sampled in research lives in dedicated 'Noms de Lieux et de Peuples' sections, but those aren't headword-shaped.
3. Longnon vol 1: 67 parser entries (only 24% accept), but the 470 pages contain ~3,500-4,200 named-place mentions in chapter prose. The headword parser misses 99% of those.

Proposal:
- New parser mode 'commentary' that finds etymology-commentary sections via heuristics (chapter heading patterns, dense Latin / 'cf.' / italic-form markers, year-citation density).
- For numbered-list shapes (saint-names, feudal-castles): segment by line-leading number ('1725.', '1726.') instead of by capital-letter headword.
- LLM-prompt variant that handles 'one-section, many-toponyms' shape (current schema is one-toponym-many-elements; would need a new 'extract-list-of-etymology-pairs' shape).

Estimated unlocked yield (rough projections):
- Longnon vol 1: 67 entries → potentially 600+ entries with section/numbered-list awareness, at 24% accept = 144+ rows (vs 16 today)
- Longnon vol 2: 2,775 → realistic ~1,500-2,000 numbered saint-name entries; even at 15% accept = 225+ rows
- Loth 1890: 615 → ~150-200 etymology-commentary entries; at 30% accept = 50+ rows
- d'Arbois 1890: ~700 entries possible, similar shape

Aggregate: easily 500+ new toponym etymology rows across these four sources.

Out of scope:
- The existing alphabetical-headword + skeat-section parsers stay unchanged for genuinely-dictionary-shaped books.
- Per-section / per-numbered-list LLM extraction is the real change; the parser is just a feeder.

OWNERSHIP NOTE: parser code is in dictionary_parser.py / skeat_parser.py / cli.py — out of the research/extractor agent's scope. Filing for the parser-side agent.

title: Expand MOODS vocabulary: pastoral, noble, mortuary, etc.
description:
The --mood preset table (__init__.py MOODS) currently has just 'grim' and 'harsh'. Per DECISIONS.md D6 the GM-facing vocabulary should grow to cover the spec-named axis: pastoral, noble, ominous, mortuary — each bundling a tag-union (and optionally a harshness default).

Why filed: the recipe shape is already in place; adding moods is mechanical (one MOODS entry + one or two seeds of test). Useful to ship more variety as soon as the lexicon's tag coverage catches up.

Scope per mood (pick the ones with corpus support; defer the rest):
- pastoral: tag union over { tree, water, plant, animal, agriculture } if those tags are present at meaningful coverage. Maybe a small negative harshness signal (or a SOFT mood that biases away from stop-final).
- noble: tag union over { religion, saint, royalty } — likely needs a 'royalty' tag added at mining time first.
- mortuary: union of { death, burial } — death exists today; 'burial' and 'mortuary' are spec'd D6 names not yet in the bundle.
- ominous: phonological + semantic (subset of grim with darker tag bias).

Acceptance:
- For each new mood added: smoke test seed=42 english produces visibly different output vs plain.
- Test parity with the existing grim/harsh tests (empty=identity, seed-stable, distribution-shifts, composes).
- Audit query first: for each candidate tag, count subjects in the bundle (avoid shipping a mood that maps to <5 morphemes).

Out of scope:
- Adding new corpus tags from mining (separate ticket if a desired mood needs them).
- A 'soft' mood that uses negative harshness — would require extending _blend_harsh to handle the soft side; design choice deferred.

Resources: PR #25 review feedback (complexity-reviewer 3177349229) suggested switching _apply_mood to a MoodEffect dataclass when a third effect axis lands; worth doing inside this ticket if any of these moods needs a non-tag, non-harshness axis (e.g. an orthography hint or a register shift).

title: D5-3: Era-aware bundle export + runtime cell selection
description:
Interface-layer of D5. Wires meanings.json + Meaning runtime to support era-cell selection at generation time.

Bundle shape (per D26 sibling-field pattern):
  Adds <lang>_era arrays carrying [{form, earliest, latest, cell}] entries per attested form.
  Example:
    'old_english_era': [
       {'form': 'tūn', 'earliest': 731, 'latest': 1066, 'cell': 'oe-late'},
       {'form': 'tun', 'earliest': 1086, 'latest': 1300, 'cell': 'me'},
       {'form': 'town', 'earliest': 1500, 'latest': null, 'cell': 'modern'}
    ]

Runtime:
- Meaning.pick_era_form(rng, era_cell) picks an attested form whose era cell matches; falls back to canonical (lang[0]) if no attestation in that cell
- NameGenerator.select(era=...) threads through and pre-renders surface substitutions at select time so __str__ stays pure
- 'load_meanings' strips _era suffix and routes into Meaning.eras

CLI:
  wyrd kenning generate english --era oe-late
  wyrd kenning generate english --era 1086        # year-as-era resolves to cell
  wyrd kenning generate english --era modern      # default-off preserves existing behavior

Update export-meanings to compute per-form era cells using D5-1's attested_year + D5-2's era_cell function.

Bundle-size budget: ~30-50 KB extra (negligible for importlib.resources path).

Determinism contract: --era=null (default) preserves bit-stable existing output. Picking --era N changes the pool; existing seeds will produce different names with --era set. This is the standard pattern (matches --novelty / --spelling-variety / --inflection-density).

Depends on D5-1 (data populated) + D5-2 (cell definitions).

See /tmp/wyrd-d5-era-axis-design-2026-05-02.md.
notes: Merged in PR #57 (squash). Code: strict era resolution + friendly error wrapper + full-coverage short-circuit. Tests: 8 new (CLI, culture mapping, error path, empty-string, _select_tag plumbing, full-coverage→None). 950 tests pass.

title: D5-2: Era-cell mapping + filtered sampling on (language × era) axis
description:
Sampling-layer of D5 era-aware register cells. Defines era cells per language family + adds '--era' CLI/JSON param that filters morpheme inventory to a chosen cell.

Era-cell definitions (proposed; see design doc):
- English: oe-early (-, 800), oe-late (800, 1100), me (1100, 1500), early-modern (1500, 1700), modern (1700, -)
- Norse: on-classical (-, 1100), on-late (1100, 1300), middle-scandinavian (1300, 1500), modern (1500, -)
- Brythonic: old (-, 1100), middle (1100, 1500), modern (1500, -)
- Goidelic: old-irish (-, 900), middle-irish (900, 1200), early-modern (1200, 1700), modern (1700, -)
- Latin: classical (-, 200), late-vulgar (200, 700), medieval (700, 1500), renaissance (1500, 1800)
- Norman-French: old-norman (-, 1300), anglo-norman (1066-1500 in England), modern (1500, -)

Implementation:
- ERA_CELLS constant in lexicon.py, keyed by family
- era_cell(language, year) -> str function
- Generator-side filter: morphemes whose attested_year falls in the chosen cell's range
- '--era' CLI argument accepts cell label OR a year (year resolves to cell)
- '--era=null' (default) preserves current bit-stable behavior

Approach for v1: era is a generation-time FILTER on the morpheme inventory; tag-co-occurrence stays per-culture (unchanged proportions JSONs). Output is 'morphemes attested in era cell, composed via culture's tag patterns.' Cheaper than a full per-(lang × era) tag-co-occurrence path; ships immediately on D5-1's data.

v2 (later): per-(lang × era) tag-co-occurrence, addressing 'tag patterns themselves shift across eras'.

Open question for the user (see design doc): is the proposed cell granularity right? Coarser (3 cells) would simplify; finer (10-year cohorts) gives more flexibility but undersamples.

See /tmp/wyrd-d5-era-axis-design-2026-05-02.md.
notes:
2026-05-02 update: User decision — era cells are PER-CULTURE, not per-language-family. Each culture defines its own ≤5 era cells, drawing era boundaries from whichever substrate languages apply. Updated proposed table:

- english: oe-early (-, 800), oe-late (800, 1100), me (1100, 1500), early-modern (1500, 1700), modern (1700, -)
- scottish: old-celtic (-, 900), middle-mixed (900, 1300), early-scots (1300, 1500), early-modern (1500, 1700), modern (1700, -)
- welsh: old-welsh (-, 1100), middle-welsh (1100, 1500), early-modern (1500, 1700), modern (1700, -) — 4 cells
- irish: old-irish (-, 900), middle-irish (900, 1200), early-modern-gaelic (1200, 1700), modern (1700, -) — 4 cells
- breton: old-breton (-, 1100), middle-breton (1100, 1700), modern (1700, -) — 3 cells (Ernault's wide moyen-breton)

ERA_CELLS dict lives in lexicon.py (or __init__.py) keyed by culture. era_cell(culture, year) -> str resolves a year inside the chosen culture's table.

Era cell labels are NOT globally unique — early-modern means 1500-1700 in english AND welsh but is absent from breton. The CLI flag '--era' is always interpreted in the context of '--culture', so 'wyrd kenning generate welsh --era middle-welsh' resolves inside welsh's table only.

User decision recap (other open questions from the design doc):
- Q1 cell granularity: 5 cells fine (some cultures use 3-4)
- Q2 axis vs enum-split: per-culture (closes the celtic-enum-split question — culture lens decides)
- Q3 default era on no-flag: keep current bit-stable behavior

See /tmp/wyrd-d5-era-axis-design-2026-05-02.md (updated 2026-05-02 with per-culture clarification).

title: D5-1: Mine attested years from source bodies via regex post-mining stage
description:
Foundation layer for D5 era-aware register cells. Adds an attested_year column to etymon_text_match and a 'lookup-attested-years' CLI step that scans source bodies for date citations near attested forms.

Approach: regex \b(\d{3,4})\b within the same sentence as a matched_form, with date-context filters (preceded by 'in'/'from'/'circa'/'DB'/'first recorded'). Idempotent / reversible (clear-enrichment --stage=attested-years).

Per D21/D22, this is enrichment-layer (LLM-free, rebuildable). No changes to mining evidence.

Schema delta:
  ALTER TABLE etymon_text_match ADD COLUMN attested_year INTEGER;
  CREATE INDEX idx_text_match_year ON etymon_text_match(attested_year);

Acceptance:
- regex extractor identifies year stamps in Mawer 1920, Ekwall 1922, Skeat county dicts (where 'X, 1086 (DB)' patterns are abundant)
- 1000+ etymon_text_match rows acquire non-null attested_year on first run
- false-positive rate <5% (validate against a 50-row sample by hand)
- idempotent re-run; clear-enrichment stage works

Foundation for D5-2 (era cell sampling) and D5-3 (era-aware bundle). Deferred year extraction during NEW mining (re-mining sources with prompt-side year capture) is a follow-up not in this ticket's scope.

See /tmp/wyrd-d5-era-axis-design-2026-05-02.md for the full architecture rationale and open questions.

title: Collapse --harsh + --grim into a unified --mood surface
description:
The two D6 knobs landed in PR #20 as separate CLI flags (--grim boolean, --harsh float). They actually skew different axes (--grim = semantic tags, --harsh = phonological weight) but the user wants them grouped under one user-facing surface — they're conceptually 'mood' presets that the GM picks rather than two unrelated dials.

Scope:
- Drop --grim and --harsh from CLI; add --mood (repeatable, choice-of-mood-names + optional :value suffix for graduation).
- Drop 'grim' boolean from JSON input_schema; KEEP 'harshness' number for graduated power-user control. Add 'mood' (array of strings).
- MOODS table in __init__.py: 'grim' -> tag-union, 'harsh' -> harshness float (default 1.0). Future moods (pastoral, noble, mortuary, etc) drop into the same table.
- 'harsh:0.5' colon syntax for graduated mood values.
- Update tests + DECISIONS D6 + README knob table.

Why this matters: the right shape for a GM-facing API. 'I want grim names' is one decision, not two. A unified mood vocabulary scales better as future moods land.

Why now: caught immediately after PR #20 landed; the user-facing surface hasn't shipped beyond the local repo, so clean-replace rather than soft-deprecate.

description:

Loth's 'Chrestomathie bretonne' is — true to its name — an ANTHOLOGY OF MIDDLE BRETON TEXTS (mystery plays, prose excerpts, manuscript folios). title: Mine Longnon 1920 vol 2 (saint-names + feudal castle names) via Haiku
description:
Volume 2 of Longnon's 'Les noms de lieu de la France' — covers saint-derived toponyms (entries 1659-2138) and feudal castle/fortress names (entry 2139+). Saint-names section alone yields hundreds of Saint-X toponyms with explicit Latin saint etymologies.

Source: archive.org/details/lesnomsdelieudel02long (874 pages, full DJVU TXT downloadable)

Tier-1 Haiku per D13. Same shape as vol 1 (which is in wyrd-efx) — feedback from a vol 1 smoke-test should inform whether vol 2 needs its own smoke first.

Adds the ecclesiastical-Latin-onto-French overlay (saint-names + feudal castle names) that vol 1's substrate-focused chapters do not cover. Combined with vol 1, French as a register becomes seriously viable.

See /tmp/wyrd-corpus-research-2026-05-02.md.
notes:
2026-05-04: 30-entry Haiku smoke against the saint-names section [1659..2138] with the new numbered-list parser (PR #65). Result: 1 accepted / 26 declined / 3 rejected — 3.3% accept rate.

Root cause is prompt mismatch, NOT parser shape. The numbered-list parser correctly segments 475 entries with 88% toponym detection. But the SYSTEM_PROMPT in llm_extractor.py is calibrated for 19th/20th-c English place-name etymology PROSE (Skeat/Mawer-style 'the etymon X means Y in Old English'), and the Longnon saint-name format is terse Latin → French derivation:

  1659. Caradocus ; Saint-Caradu (Côtes-du-Nord, Morbihan), Saint-Cadreuc (...).

The LLM treats this as 'no etymology' (sets found=false / decline) because there's no narrative explanation of the derivation; it's a one-line cross-reference shape. title: Wire D6 (--harsh + --grim): orthogonal name-flavor filters
description:
DECISIONS.md D6 specifies two orthogonal filters that apply to ANY language: --harsh is phonological skew (short syllables, harsh consonant clusters, voiced-stop endings), --grim is a semantic-tag filter (grim/mortuary/monstrous/battle/wilderness). Together they let a GM ask for menacing-feeling Slavic-east names without the engine pre-coding any culture as 'orcish'.

Currently neither exists. The phonology data is in wyrd/generators/kenning/phonology.py but isn't wired to a generation skew.

Scope:
1. --grim implementation: it's a multi-tag union filter ('any of grim/mortuary/monstrous/battle/wilderness'). Mostly a CLI sugar on top of existing --tag. But: requires those tags to actually exist in the lexicon at meaningful coverage. Probe the data first; might surface gaps.
2. --harsh implementation: a phonological score per morpheme (high = harsh, low = soft) computed from the language's phonology table at proportions-load time. Generation re-weights the empirical proportions by harsh_score^harshness_strength. Knob 0..1.
3. CLI: 'wyrd kenning generate english --harsh --grim --culture slavic-east' (forward-compat for a slavic-east register).
4. Braitham Gate test: at harsh=0 + grim=False, behavior unchanged.
5. Smoke test: harsh=1 + grim produces visibly menacing names that ARE still well-formed (location keys etc.)

Acceptance: filters compose orthogonally; existing English-Welsh-Scottish-Irish all work with both; CLI and JSON schema both expose them.
notes:
Audit 2026-05-02: the D6-spec'd tag names ('grim', 'mortuary', 'monstrous', 'battle', 'wilderness') don't exist in the corpus today. Closest existing tags after the lexicon-bundle regen:
  death (18 subjects), military (27), monster (8), undead (9), magic (4).
The --grim implementation should map to a composable union of existing tags, with the original D6 tag names left as future-mining targets (a 'grim' tag could be added at mining time once we have a Tier-2 review pass that retags morphemes with affect labels). Suggested initial mapping: --grim = death OR military OR monster OR undead OR magic.

--harsh side is independent: needs a phonological score per morpheme computed from phonology.py tables. No data dependency outside what's already in the bundle.

title: Wire D8: generator composes <lemma>@<inflection> from lexicon data
description:
DECISIONS.md D8 commits to inflection-aware generation: pick a lemma, pick an inflection, surface the appropriate form. Currently the runtime sees flat usage strings and has no concept of inflection — the lemma_id + inflection columns in the lexicon don't reach generation.

Scope:

2. Runtime: extend Meaning class to track which forms in 'sources' are inflected variants vs the lemma. title: Wire D18: spelling variant sampling at generation time

title: Wire D17: Bayesian mixture sampling + --novelty knob in name generation
description:
Per DECISIONS.md D17, name generation should sample from a mixture: alpha*empirical-pair-frequency + beta*tag-class-prior + gamma*marginal. The --novelty knob shifts weight toward gamma to allow plausible-but-unattested combinations. The Braitham Gate regression test pins the empirical end ('descriptive+topography compound first-word' must remain producible at default settings).

Currently proportions.py:Generator.select() does pure empirical-frequency weighted_choice — no tag-class prior, no marginal blending, no novelty parameter.

Scope:
1. Compute tag-class priors and marginals once at proportions-load time. Tag co-occurrence is already tracked in proportions JSON per D16 (tag_cooccurrence + tag_marginal Counters in cli.py:_proportions_from). Surface them on the runtime side via load_proportions.
2. Blend at MeaningGenerator.select() via mixture: novelty alpha=0 -> pure empirical; alpha=1 -> pure marginal. Default 0.0 (current behavior).
3. Expose 'novelty' in Kenning.input_schema as a 0..1 float. Plumb through generate(params, seed).
4. CLI: 'wyrd kenning generate --novelty 0.3 english' etc.
5. Braitham Gate regression test: at novelty=0 a known-attested compound shape must still be producible.
6. Novelty regression test: at novelty=1 generation must still produce well-formed (location-key compatible) names — no schema violation.

Acceptance: novelty 0 reproduces today's behavior bit-for-bit on the same seed; novelty 1 produces visibly different distribution with no malformed names; Braitham Gate test passes; new test pins novelty=0.5 produces a stable seed-deterministic output.

title: Per-language witness thresholds in export-meanings
description:
Currently export-meanings uses a uniform --min-witnesses N (default 3) across all languages. The corpus availability differs hugely by language: old-english has 32 mined sources and 2118 lemmas at ≥1 witness, while old-norse has effectively one focused dictionary (Lindkvist 1912) and the structural ceiling at ≥3 witnesses is 43 ON lemmas. A uniform 3-witness gate filters out 93% of ON, mostly for corpus-thinness reasons rather than quality.

Quality spot-check at w=2 (per-language samples drawn 2026-05-02):
- old-english: ~80% clean (some Tier-1 prose-extraction noise like 'row' glossed as 'clearing')
- celtic: ~90% clean (dearg, meen, eidnedin all real)
- old-norse: ~95% clean (hylr, haukr, bygging, blá, kirkja all real)
- modern-english: 100% clean (mill, stone, head, east, hall)
- norman-french: 100% clean (blanche, lieu, castle, monte)
- latin: 100% clean (ecclesia, ceaster, monasterium)
- biblical: 100% clean (asa, asaph saint names)

Recommended preset:
- old-english: 3 (well-mined; strict gate keeps OE Tier-1 noise out)
- celtic: 2 (mining structurally harder per D13)
- old-norse: 2 (corpus structurally thin)
- modern-english: 2
- norman-french: 2

Net effect: ~+377 lemmas vs uniform w=3, mostly Celtic (+278) and ON (+75).

title: Make enrichment fully reversible: non-destructive OCR clustering + method-version stamps on derived rows
description:
Why this exists:

User wants to iterate on enrichment logic (lemma linking, OCR clustering, text-match search) without losing mining data. Mining is expensive ($/time); enrichment is cheap. We need 'blow away enrichment, re-run with new logic, keep canonical mining data intact' as a one-liner workflow.

Today, two of three enrichment stages are already reversible (link-lemmas via column resets; text-match via DELETE). The third (normalize-ocr) is destructive — it merges redundant etymons by DELETE-ing the loser, so once merged, you can't roll back without re-mining.

What needs to be done:

1. Non-destructive OCR clustering:

   Schema change: ALTER TABLE etymon ADD COLUMN merged_into_id INTEGER REFERENCES etymon(id) ON DELETE SET NULL.

   When cluster_ocr_variants merges two etymons:
   - Repoint citations/glosses/tags to winner (existing logic)
   - SET losers.merged_into_id = winner_id (new — instead of DELETE)
   - DON'T delete the loser row

   A SQL view exposes the canonical set:
     CREATE VIEW etymon_canonical AS
       SELECT * FROM etymon WHERE merged_into_id IS NULL;

   All consumers query etymon_canonical instead of etymon. The merged-loser rows preserve history (their canonical_form, original glosses/tags pre-merge if we move them).

   Blow-away to re-run clustering:
     UPDATE etymon SET merged_into_id = NULL;
     -- then re-run normalize-ocr with whatever new heuristic

2. Method+version stamps on derived rows:

   ALTER TABLE etymon_text_match ADD COLUMN method TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'reverse-search-v1';
   -- 'reverse-search-v1', 'fuzzy-search-v1', 'llm-disambiguated-v1', etc.

   ALTER TABLE etymon ADD COLUMN lemma_method TEXT;
   -- NULL if not linked, else 'link-lemmas-v1' etc.

   Blow-away CLI subcommands:
     wyrd kenning lexicon clear-enrichment --stage=text-match     # DELETE etymon_text_match
     wyrd kenning lexicon clear-enrichment --stage=lemmas         # NULL out lemma_id/inflection/lemma_method
     wyrd kenning lexicon clear-enrichment --stage=ocr            # NULL out merged_into_id
     wyrd kenning lexicon clear-enrichment --stage=all-derived    # all three

3. Update the post-mining chain script (/tmp/post-mining-pipeline.sh) to optionally start with a clear-enrichment step:
     wyrd kenning lexicon clear-enrichment --stage=all-derived
     wyrd kenning lexicon link-lemmas --apply
     wyrd kenning lexicon normalize-ocr --apply
     ...

4. Document the canonical/derived distinction in DECISIONS.md (proposed D-next):
   - Canonical: source, etymon (excl. lemma_id/inflection/merged_into_id), etymon_citation, etymon_gloss, etymon_tag, toponym, toponym_etymology, toponym_etymology_element, toponym_attestation. Mining writes; enrichment never modifies.
   - Derived: etymon.lemma_id/inflection/merged_into_id columns + etymon_text_match. Enrichment writes; can be cleared and re-run safely.

Acceptance criteria:
- Running clear-enrichment then re-running the post-mining chain produces the same final state as running the chain on a fresh DB (modulo non-determinism in LLM-disambiguator if introduced).
- A test that mines + enriches + clear-enrichments + re-enriches yields the same canonical row counts.
- normalize-ocr no longer DELETEs etymon rows; merged-loser rows are queryable for provenance.
- The bug fix from wyrd-go5 (cluster_ocr_variants missing FK repoints) is moot once non-destructive merge lands — there's no DELETE that can fail.

Soft prereqs: none. Supersedes wyrd-go5 (the merge-FK bug becomes irrelevant when we stop deleting).
close_reason: Merged via PR #7 (commit 64a99c9). Non-destructive OCR clustering via merged_into_id, two-step rollup in etymon_consensus, clear-enrichment CLI for ocr/lemmas/text-match/all-derived stages, method/version stamps on derived rows. wyrd-7lo (P3) tracks the follow-up canonical rollup views for etymon_gloss/tag/text_match. Supersedes wyrd-go5's interim fix and obviates wyrd-1pl.

title: LLM-disambiguator pass for ambiguous fuzzy-search candidates (Tier 2 review on text-match collisions)
description:
Why this exists:

The reverse-search / fuzzy-search pipeline finds candidate text-matches between lexicon etymons and source body strings. The current discriminator (Levenshtein ≤ 1 + gloss-anchor heuristic, D15) produces false positives when the gloss-anchor word is generic ('land', 'area', 'district' — see wyrd-c3x for the herath ↔ heath case). Stricter heuristics help but don't fully resolve the problem; some cases require actual semantic understanding of the surrounding text.

LLM disambiguation is the right substrate for this: small candidate set, bounded context, multiple-choice answer, verifiable output. Tier 2 territory per D2 (Gemini Flash).

What needs to be done:

1. Rebuild fuzzy-search as a two-stage pipeline:
   - Stage 1 (heuristic, cheap): produce a candidate-set per body-text hit. For surface form X, find all lexicon etymons within edit distance ≤ 1 (preserving D15 gloss-anchor as a soft-include signal but not the hard gate).
   - Stage 2 (LLM disambiguator, only when candidate-set size > 1 OR gloss is generic OR cross-check finds X already exists as a canonical etymon): pass to Tier 2 model.

2. Disambiguator prompt structure:
   - 200-char snippet around the body hit
   - N candidate etymons formatted as: 'A: <canonical_form> (<language>) — <glosses>; tags: <tags>'
   - Question: 'In the passage above, the word X appears. Which of these morphemes (if any) is being described or used? Reply with one of A/B/C/.../none, plus a one-sentence reason.'
   - JSON-schema-constrained output: {choice: 'A'|'B'|...|'none', confidence: 'high'|'medium'|'low', reason: str}

3. Form-in-body validation (D3): the chosen etymon's canonical form must appear in the snippet (already true by construction since it's a fuzzy match). Also: confidence='low' answers don't get ingested as text-match rows; they get logged for review.

4. Storage: same etymon_text_match table, but with a new column source_method ('regex' | 'fuzzy' | 'llm-disambiguated') for provenance. Notes column carries the LLM's reasoning string.

5. Cost gate: skip the LLM call entirely when (candidate-set size == 1) AND (the candidate is not also a canonical etymon for the surface form). The vast majority of hits don't need it.

6. Cleanup of existing false positives: run an audit pass on existing etymon_text_match rows. For each row whose matched_form is itself a canonical etymon (different from row.etymon_id), flag and re-run through the disambiguator. The herath ↔ heath case from 2026-05-01 is the canonical example.

Acceptance criteria:
- A regression test: feeding the herath/heath snippet to the disambiguator returns 'heath is being used here, not herath' (with the canonical heath etymon picked, not the ON district term).
- Disambiguator-routed text-match rows are tagged with source_method='llm-disambiguated' and the model's reasoning is queryable.
- A test asserting the cost gate: when candidate-set size = 1 and surface != canonical-etymon-for-X, no LLM call is made.

Soft prereqs: none — bug fix + architecture refinement on existing pipeline.
Supersedes: wyrd-c3x's heuristic-only fix path (or runs alongside; the heuristic improvements still reduce LLM call volume).
notes:
Refinement (2026-05-01, per user): the disambiguator must be able to request MORE text context when the initial snippet isn't sufficient.

Why: a 200-char window is sometimes too narrow. A morpheme ambiguity might be resolved by the section heading two paragraphs up, or by a definition in the preceding sentence chain. Letting the model request what it needs is cleaner than picking a fixed window and hoping.

Architectural shape: agentic disambiguator. The model's response is a discriminated union:

  {action: 'answer', choice, confidence, reason}                  # final
  {action: 'request_more_context', direction, chars}              # ask for more

Where direction in {'before', 'after', 'both'} and chars is the additional window to add (capped per-call, e.g. ≤ 500). The orchestrator honors the request, expands the snippet, and re-prompts. Iteration cap: 3 expansion rounds or 2000 chars total context, whichever first. Beyond that, the model is forced to commit ('answer' or 'none').

Implementation:

1. Tool-call style with Anthropic / Gemini structured-output:
   - Tool 1: `expand_context(direction, chars)` returns the wider snippet.
   - Tool 2: `commit_answer(choice, confidence, reason)` is the terminal call.
   - Orchestrator runs the conversation loop; tracks expansion history per case.

2. Per-case logging: how many expansions the model needed, total chars consumed, final commit. Useful for tuning the heuristic gate (cases that always need expansion → bump the default starting window for that pattern).

3. Cost: each expansion is another LLM call but small. Cap at 3 rounds × ~500 tokens each = ~1500 tokens per ambiguous case. Still pennies at Tier 2 rates.

4. Acceptance criterion update: a test case with deliberate need-for-more-context. Seed a passage where the first 200 chars is genuinely ambiguous but the next 300 chars resolves it (e.g., 'the heath here, an upland district' — disambiguates herath vs heath only when 'an upland district' is included). Disambiguator should request expansion and arrive at the correct answer.

New CLI: wyrd kenning lexicon disambiguate-fuzzy. Schema: disambiguator_reason column on etymon_text_match. D25 added. Follow-ups: wyrd-uct (agentic expand_context) and wyrd-9ae (group cases by source/matched_form).

title: fuzzy-search: gloss-anchor too permissive on generic gloss words (false positive: herath ↔ heath)
description:
Why this is broken:

Audit case (2026-05-01): the fuzzy-search step matched ON 'herath' (= ON herað, 'district/county/region') to body-text 'heath' (= OE hǣþ, 'untilled land') with edit_distance=1, anchored by herath's glosses 'land', 'area', 'district'. 47 false-positive hits across 5 sources before the audit caught it.

The two morphemes are completely unrelated etymologically (ON herað vs OE hǣþ) but the gloss anchor fired because 'land', 'area', 'district' are generic words that frequently appear in scholarly toponym discussion near words like 'heath'.

D15 currently says: fuzzy edit-distance ≤ 1 only counts when a gloss-string from etymon_gloss appears within ~100 characters of the matched form. The intent is to prevent bere/bera (barley/bear) coincidences. The implementation works for specific glosses but fails on generic ones that co-occur with many topographic words.

What needs to be done:

Two refinements (probably both):

(1) Gloss specificity weighting:
- Tag gloss strings with a specificity score. 'fortified hilltop settlement' = high; 'land' / 'area' / 'place' = low.
- Require the gloss anchor to hit at least one high-specificity gloss, OR a specific multi-word phrase, OR two co-occurring glosses in the window.
- Alternatively: maintain a stop-word list of low-discriminating glosses ('land', 'area', 'district', 'place', 'settlement') that don't count as anchors on their own.

(2) Cross-check against existing etymons:
- Before accepting 'X is a fuzzy variant of Y' (where Y is canonical), run a reverse-search lookup on X. If X exists as its own canonical etymon already, skip the fuzzy-variant claim entirely — X is X, not a variant of Y.
- This alone would have suppressed the herath ↔ heath case since 'heath' is an etymon (id 2106).

Cleanup:
- Run a one-shot DELETE from etymon_text_match WHERE the matched_form points at an etymon that exists in the lexicon as its own canonical_form, and the row's etymon_id (claimed source) is a different etymon. These are the exact false-positive shape.

Acceptance criteria:
- The herath ↔ heath rows are removed from etymon_text_match.
- A regression test seeds two etymons (one specific, one generic-glossed) and asserts the generic-glossed one does NOT fuzzy-match a body word that's a canonical etymon in its own right.
- D15 in DECISIONS.md gets a paragraph appended documenting the gloss-specificity refinement.
close_reason: Fixed: fuzzy_search_attestations now skips matches where the body token is itself a canonical etymon. 131 false-positive rows deleted from etymon_text_match. Regression test in test_kenning_lexicon.py. D15 in DECISIONS.md updated with the structural-cross-check refinement.

title: cluster_ocr_variants drops 2 FKs: etymon.lemma_id self-FK and etymon_text_match
description:
Why this is broken:

After running `wyrd kenning lexicon link-lemmas --apply` (which sets etymon.lemma_id on inflected variants pointing at lemmas) followed by `wyrd kenning lexicon normalize-ocr --apply`, the OCR clustering hits FOREIGN KEY constraint failed on DELETE FROM etymon WHERE id = ?

Reproduction: post-mining chain run on 2026-05-01. Step 1 linked 106 inflected variants; step 2 immediately failed.

Root cause:

cluster_ocr_variants (lexicon.py around line 1041) repoints these references before deleting the loser etymon:
- etymon_citation
- etymon_gloss
- etymon_tag
- reflex_etymon
- toponym_etymology_element

It MISSES:
1. etymon.lemma_id self-FK — inflected children of the loser still reference it via lemma_id. The DELETE fails.
2. etymon_text_match — has ON DELETE CASCADE so it doesn't block the delete, but cascading drops the text-match rows that should be repointed to the winner.

What needs to be done:

Add two more repoint statements before the DELETE:

```python
# Re-parent inflected children of the loser to the winner.
db.conn.execute(
    "UPDATE etymon SET lemma_id = ? WHERE lemma_id = ?",
    (winner_id, loser_id),
)

# Repoint text-match rows (UNIQUE on etymon_id+source_id+matched_form, so
# use INSERT OR IGNORE then delete originals; or just UPDATE since the
# UNIQUE conflict is the only risk).
db.conn.execute(
    "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO etymon_text_match (etymon_id, source_id, matched_form, match_count, edit_distance, snippet) "
    "SELECT ?, source_id, matched_form, match_count, edit_distance, snippet FROM etymon_text_match WHERE etymon_id = ?",
    (winner_id, loser_id),
)
db.conn.execute(
    "DELETE FROM etymon_text_match WHERE etymon_id = ?",
    (loser_id,),
)
```

Then DELETE FROM etymon proceeds cleanly.

Acceptance criteria:
- post-mining chain runs end to end without FK violation.
- A regression test covering: (a) lemma row that's a cluster-loser correctly re-parents inflected children to the winner before deletion; (b) text-match rows survive the merge attached to the winner; (c) UNIQUE constraints on text-match are respected (no duplicate rows after merge).
- Schema-level safety: consider FOREIGN KEY ... ON DELETE RESTRICT on etymon.lemma_id so future omissions fail loud rather than silent.

Soft prereq: none — bug fix in existing code.
notes: Likely superseded by wyrd-et0 (non-destructive OCR clustering). If we stop DELETE-ing etymon rows in normalize-ocr (mark-as-merged instead), the FK constraint failure becomes impossible — there's no DELETE that can fail. Keep this ticket open as a fallback path: if wyrd-et0 stalls, the two-line FK repoint fix in wyrd-go5 is still the right interim patch. Close wyrd-go5 once wyrd-et0 lands.
close_reason: Merged via PR #5 (commit 21f6810). FK repoint logic in cluster_ocr_variants now covers etymon.lemma_id self-FK and etymon_text_match; mining-evidence-preserving UPSERT sums match_counts on collision per D21.

title: Name Lab: composable transform pipeline for branching/scrubbing name evolution
description:
Why this exists:

Generation produces a name; the explainer decomposes it. The Name Lab is a third mode: take a name (generated, decomposed, or user-supplied) and apply surgical transforms to produce variant names. Each transform is composable, undoable, branchable. Result is a UX where a worldbuilder can generate, explore, refine, and commit names — with the linguistic substrate doing the consistency work.

The lab is the culmination of the lexicon project's worldbuilding ambition. Generation alone gives a single roll; the lab gives the GM the alternate-history kin of any given name (Bridgewater + time-warp -3 = Brycgwæter; + harsh +2 = Britwart; + calque ON = Brúvatn) and lets them pick, branch, or compose further.

What needs to be done:

1. Lab data model:
   - LabSession holds a tree of Names: root (initial generation or user input) + branches (post-transform variants).
   - Each Name carries (surface_form, decomposition, applied_transforms[], parent_id).
   - Transforms are pure functions: (Name, lexicon, params) -> [(candidate_Name, score)] — so a transform with multiple plausible outputs returns the top-N.
   - LabSession serializable to JSON for persistence.

2. Transform categories and the specific transforms in each:

   PHONOLOGICAL (uses wyrd-4i6 rules library):
   - homophone_shift: apply one or more phonological mutation rules (vowel shift, C↔G/K/S consonant variants, palatalization). Probabilistically — surface forms vary by historical likelihood.
   - time_warp(direction='back', steps=N): apply inverse rules N times to age the form backward (modern -> ME -> OE -> PGmc).
   - time_warp(direction='forward', steps=N): apply forward rules N times to project newer.

   MORPHOLOGICAL:
   - inflect(morpheme_index, inflection): change one morpheme's inflectional form (cot -> cotan -> cotum).
   - replace_morpheme(morpheme_index, new_etymon_id): swap one slot for a specific etymon (manual override).
   - reroll_morpheme(morpheme_index): re-draw one slot from the current generator pool (your #4).
   - meaning_preserving_swap(morpheme_index): replace with a candidate sharing at least one synset (your #5; uses wyrd-7tz).
   - affix_stack(suffix_morpheme): layer a productive suffix (X -> X-ham -> X-hampton -> X-hamptonshire) (#9).
   - affix_strip: peel one layer off.
   - position_swap(i, j): reorder two morphemes (#10).
   - hypocoristic / augmentative: diminutive vs grand form (#11).
   - tautology_layer(language=X): add a same-synset morpheme from language X — produces Pendle Hill / Table Mesa shapes.

   CROSS-LANGUAGE (uses wyrd-7tz):
   - calque(target_language): translate every morpheme's meaning into target language equivalents (#6).
   - anglicize: pull all morphemes into English (replace foreign morphemes with English-equivalent synset members) (#7).
   - foreignize(target_language): mirror — pull into the target language fully.

   ORTHOGRAPHIC (uses wyrd-4i6 + scribal-era rules):
   - era_spelling_shift(target_era): same morphemes, surface form respelled per target era's scribal conventions. Distinct from time_warp because the underlying morphology stays put — just orthography (#8).

   STYLISTIC ('drift toward'):
   - drift_harsh: apply one rule from the --harsh package (short syllables, voiceless onsets, consonant-cluster endings).
   - drift_archaic: apply one inverse-time-warp step.
   - drift_norse_coded: replace one OE morpheme with its ON cognate or synset-equivalent.
   - drift_register(register): walk one step toward a packaged register (formal/folk, urban/pastoral, etc.).

3. Composition:
   - Chain: lab.apply(transform_a).apply(transform_b)...
   - Branch: lab.branch_at(name_id).apply(transform_c)
   - Undo: lab.undo() (walk parent_id chain back one step)
   - Diff: lab.diff(name_a, name_b) — show transform path from a to b
   - History view: tree of all names visited in this session

4. Each transform reports:
   - delta description ('time_warp -1 step: applied OE → ME palatalization rule')
   - which morphemes changed
   - whether the result crosses the realistic→fictional boundary (any morpheme now carries 'fiction' tag → result is fiction-tagged)
   - quality score — composite of (morpheme attestation, sound-shift rule confidence, decomposition canonical-fit per wyrd-08m)

5. CLI surface:
   wyrd kenning lab generate <culture>          # roll initial name into lab
   wyrd kenning lab from <name>                 # bring an existing name in
   wyrd kenning lab apply <transform> [args]    # apply transform to current
   wyrd kenning lab branch                      # branch at current
   wyrd kenning lab show                        # tree view
   wyrd kenning lab commit <name_id>            # finalize and exit lab

6. SPA surface (later, optional): visualize the branching tree, click-to-apply transforms.

Acceptance criteria:
- Each transform category has at least one regression test on a known seed: e.g., time_warp(-3) on 'Bridgewater' produces 'brycgwæter' or close variant.
- A composition test: chain three transforms, undo, branch, apply different transform — final state is correct and reproducible.
- The fiction-tag boundary is honored: applying calque(target=constructed-greek) on a realistic name produces a fiction-tagged result; downstream realistic-mode draws don't see it.
- The Braitham Gate canonical decomposition stays a valid lab seed (regression coverage for the project's flagship name).

Hard prereqs (deps):
- wyrd-k8e: trie matcher (re-decompose surface forms post-transform)
- wyrd-08m: decomposition multiplicity (transform may unlock new candidate breakdowns)
- wyrd-7tz: synset layer (meaning-preserving + cross-language transforms)
- wyrd-yan: fiction tag (transform-crosses-realism boundary)
- wyrd-4i6: sound-change rules library (phonological + time-warp + orthographic transforms)

Implementation order suggestion (each transform is independently shippable):
- Phase 1: morphological transforms (replace, reroll, swap, position) — leans on existing matcher; lowest substrate risk.
- Phase 2: meaning-preserving + cross-language — requires wyrd-7tz.
- Phase 3: phonological + time-warp + orthographic — requires wyrd-4i6.
- Phase 4: stylistic 'drift toward' packs — composes the above.
- Phase 5: SPA visualization.

title: Sound-change rules library: forward and inverse phonological transforms per language/era
description:
Why this exists:

Several upcoming transforms need a packaged library of phonological sound-change rules:

- Lab transform #2 (homophone mutation): vowel shifts (Great Vowel Shift OE/ME/ModE), consonant variants (C↔G↔K↔S in scribal practice and Norman influence), palatalization (k→ch in OE -ic > -ich).
- Lab transform #3 (time warp): forward = apply rules in chronological order to age a form; inverse = walk rules backward to derive a candidate older form.
- Cross-language transforms (calque, foreignize): need to apply the borrowing-era's sound shifts when introducing a foreign morpheme.
- Modern→historical reverse-engineering (the 'inverse-degrade' direction discussed earlier): inverse application of these rules with backtracking.

Currently `phonology.py` only does OCR ligature normalization (æ↔cs/ce, ð↔§). It's the natural home for the sound-change rules but doesn't have them yet.

What needs to be done:

1. Encode rules per (language, era_from, era_to) tuples. Rule shape:
   - regex pattern matching the input form
   - replacement template
   - environment constraints (e.g., 'only in stressed syllable', 'only word-final')
   - probability weight (for stochastic application — some rules are universal, some sporadic)

2. Coverage targets:
   - OE → ME → ModE: ~30-50 productive rules. Vowel shifts, palatalization, syncope, lenition of intervocalic fricatives, -tūn → -ton, -hām → -ham, æ → e/a, þ → th, ð → th/d.
   - PGmc → OE: ~15 rules for inverse derivation (i-mutation, breaking, smoothing).
   - ON → modern reflex (in English): ~10 rules covering the Norse loanword chain.
   - Welsh / Brythonic → modern (mostly orthography rules, a few mutations).
   - Latin → vernacular (medieval scribal Latinization rules; mostly for explaining attestation chains).

3. API surface:
   - apply_rules(form, language, from_era, to_era, mode='forward'|'inverse') -> list[(form, probability)]
   - canonical chain: forward(forward(form, OE, ME), ME, ModE) === forward(form, OE, ModE)
   - inverse takes a modern form and returns probability-weighted candidate ancestors

4. Each rule documented with:
   - human-readable description
   - exemplar input → output pair from the corpus (e.g., 'OE brycg → ModE bridge via velar palatalization')
   - bibliographic source (Smith Elements, Campbell OE Grammar, etc.)

5. Unit tests with worked examples per rule. Particular care on inverse application — the rule set must produce the historically attested form for at least one test corpus per language pair.

Acceptance criteria:
- 30+ rules for OE→ME→ModE forward chain.
- Inverse application of the OE→ModE chain on 20 known test toponyms produces the attested OE form within the top-3 candidates for >70% of cases.
- A test confirms apply_rules('Bridgewater', 'old-english', 'modern-english', mode='inverse') includes 'brycgwæter' or close variant in its candidate set.

Soft prereqs: none — this is foundation work standalone.
notes:
2026-05-02 update (research session reference-monograph survey): Re-scoped after probing Sweet 1888 / Morris-Jones 1913 / Noreen 1903. The reference monographs are NOT directly mineable as YAML rules.

Sweet 1888 (archive.org/details/historyofenglish00sweeuoft, ~280 pages with word-list): TOC has clean period sections (OE p.99, ME p.154, ModE p.199), but uses prose-with-examples + parenthetical Romic notation, not formal rules. Sample: 'The change of (ii) into (ai) and (uu) into (au) respectively begins with slight lowering of first half'.

Morris-Jones 1913 (archive.org/details/welshgrammarhist00morr, 524p): organized by SOUND CATEGORY (vowel changes, consonant changes), NOT by period. Historical-comparative integrates examples across Old/Middle/Modern Welsh within each sound topic. Even harder to mine mechanically than Sweet.

Noreen 1903 3rd ed (archive.org/details/altislndischeun04noregoog, 446p, German): standard Lautlehre/Flexionslehre shape. German requires translation pass for any extraction.

Updated scope:
v1: Hand-curate ~30-50 rules per (language × era-transition) cell — English (OE→ME, ME→EModE, EModE→ModE) + Welsh (OW→ModW). Bounded scope; well-documented.
v2: LLM-assisted prose-to-rule extraction from Sweet/Morris-Jones/Noreen for coverage gaps. Use Sonnet 4.6 — exactly the runtime-quality LLM budget D19 reserved.
v3: Per-culture overrides (Scots-specific changes vs southern English).

NO mining ticket needed for the reference monographs themselves. They are references, not data sources for the existing mining pipeline.

Rule format proposal (YAML, per design doc):
  old-english_to_middle-english:
    vowel_lengthening:
      - {pattern: ū, replacement: ou, context: stressed}
    consonant_palatalization:
      - {pattern: c, replacement: ch, context: before_front_vowel}

Lives alongside phonology.py with derive_form(form, lang, from_era, to_era). See /tmp/wyrd-research-followups-2026-05-02.md.

title: Synset layer: cross-language meaning-preserving morpheme equivalence graph
description:
Why this exists:

Several upcoming generator transforms need a cross-connected library of same-meaning morphemes across languages and registers. Examples:
- Lab transform 'replace one root with another' (meaning-preserving): swap OE wæter for OE strēam (both 'flowing water'), or for ON bekkr (cross-language calque), but NOT for OE mere (body of water — different sense).
- Calque transform: White Hill → Albus Mons (Latin) → Hvíthóll (ON) → Bryn Gwyn (Welsh). Requires meaning-anchored cross-language morpheme equivalence.
- Anglicize / Foreignize: pull a mixed-language name fully into one language by replacing each morpheme with its same-meaning equivalent in the target language.
- Drift toward Norse-coded: replace one OE morpheme with its ON cognate or semantic-equivalent.

The current data layer covers part of this:
- etymon_tag does coarse clustering (water, hill, tree, monster) but is too broad — 'water' conflates body / flowing / precipitation / crossable.
- reflex_etymon captures cross-language convergence on the modern surface (-bury from both ON býr and OE byrh) but is anchored to surface, not meaning.
- etymon_gloss is free-text English glosses, not indexed for synonym lookup.

What's missing: fine-grained, language-invariant synonym sets — a WordNet-shape graph at the morpheme level.

What needs to be done:

1. Schema:
   CREATE TABLE synset (
     id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
     canonical_label TEXT NOT NULL,    -- 'water/flowing', 'hill/rounded', 'enclosure/farmstead'
     hypernym_id INTEGER REFERENCES synset(id),  -- hierarchy: 'water/flowing' -> 'water'
     notes TEXT
   );
   CREATE TABLE etymon_synset (
     etymon_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES etymon(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
     synset_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES synset(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
     fit TEXT CHECK (fit IN ('core', 'peripheral')),
     PRIMARY KEY (etymon_id, synset_id)
   );

2. Seed the synset catalog from existing tags + glosses. Initial set ~50-100 synsets covering the high-frequency place-name semantic classes:
   - water/flowing, water/body, water/crossable, water/spring
   - hill/rounded, hill/steep, hill/ridge, hill/pass
   - enclosure/farmstead, enclosure/fortified, enclosure/manor
   - dwelling/cottage, dwelling/hall, dwelling/temple
   - landscape/wood, landscape/clearing, landscape/grove, landscape/heath, landscape/marsh
   - direction/north, direction/south, etc.
   - colour/white, colour/black, etc.
   - tree/oak, tree/ash, tree/willow, etc. (each tree species is its own synset, not 'tree')
   - creature/dragon, creature/giant, creature/wolf, etc.

3. LLM-assisted member assignment pass:
   - For each existing etymon, propose synset memberships using tags + glosses.
   - Validate via 'every member of a synset must share at least one tag-string OR gloss-string token with the canonical_label'.
   - Mark fit='core' if the synset is the etymon's primary sense; 'peripheral' otherwise.

4. Maintenance: as mining adds new etymons (wyrd-3qq follow-up Celtic mining, wyrd-ami fantasy register, wyrd-0ab bestiary), each new etymon gets synset assignments.

5. Acquisition note: Smith's English Place-Name Elements (1956, 2 vols) is essentially a pre-built synset catalog for English/ON place-name vocabulary. If we ever acquire and OCR it, the existing entries map directly to synset rows with rich citations. Worth flagging for future scoping.

6. Generator integration:
   - Transform #5 (replace root): query for candidate morphemes sharing at least one synset (preferably 'core' fit) with the target morpheme.
   - Calque transform: walk synsets across languages.
   - Anglicize / Foreignize: same, restricted to target language.
   - Drift-toward-X: weighted draws prefer synsets where target morpheme's language is X.

Acceptance criteria:
- Synset table seeded with 50+ synsets covering ~80% of toponym-relevant semantic classes.
- Every existing etymon with at least one tag or gloss is assigned to at least one synset (or marked 'unclassified').
- Query: given an etymon-id, return all 'meaning-preserving replacement candidates' across languages and registers, with fit-score.
- A regression test: 'OE wæter has water/flowing in its synsets' AND 'OE mere does NOT share water/flowing with wæter (mere is in water/body)'.

Soft prereqs: wyrd-yan (the fiction tag) — synsets are language-invariant but the realistic vs fictional distinction stays at the tag layer; transforms compose synset query + tag filter cleanly.
