title: Personal-name etymology + naming-system clustering for NPC and player-character names
description:
Why this exists:

Place-name etymology (the rest of the kenning project) and personal-name etymology are different problems. Personal names cluster by naming-system: Sakuachi/Sialuk/Seshu sound like a family because they share phonotactics, gender-marking patterns, and morpheme inventory. The productive rules to generate more names from a cluster are extractable from a small sample.

Pathfinder NPC corpus (pfsrd2-data) contains ~48 proper-name NPCs scattered across adventure paths plus thousands of role-template NPCs. Some have rich character lore explicitly naming the culture/geography (Sakuachi: 'youngest scion in a long line of Erutaki seers...Aaminiut, a small town on the Crown of the World'). Others have nothing.

What needs to be done:

1. Cluster the proper-name NPCs by naming-system, using:
   - Lore-text cultural attribution where available ('Erutaki seer', 'Tian aristocrat', 'Garundi merchant')
   - Phonotactic similarity as a fallback (Sakuachi/Sialuk/Seshu cluster)
   - Source adventure path / setting region

2. Bucket per cluster:
   - A — real-language naming system: Greek-style names, OE/ON heroic names, Latinate Italian, Slavic. Etymology lookup via Wiktionary + Behind the Name (which has rich personal-name etymology data, possibly licensable or fair-use mineable).
   - B — constructed-in-style-of-real: pseudo-Greek, pseudo-Norse, pseudo-Welsh in PF settings. Productive rules extractable from cluster samples; etymology authored as 'analyzable as <real-language>-shape'.
   - C — pure invention: name-clusters with no real-world analog (Vornen, Dronuk, Inizkar). Productive rules from cluster phonotactics; constructed etymology with invented PIE/Sanskrit roots.

3. Apply D7 sensitivity heuristic per cluster:
   - Erutaki = Inuit-coded (active sovereignty) → framework only. Don't bundle Inuit-language data; provide the slot for community-supplied data.
   - Tian = Chinese-coded → bundle (large active-community but ancient-civilization framing applies; verify with user).
   - Mwangi = Bantu-coded (varies by community) → ask before bundling specific subclusters.
   - Vudrani = Indian-coded → similar nuance.
   - Cheliax / Taldor / Andoran etc. = European-coded → bundle freely.

4. Productive-rule extraction per accepted cluster:
   - Phonotactic constraints (allowed onset/coda clusters, vowel sets)
   - Affix inventory (Erutaki -k/-aq genitive shapes, Tian-Min syllable structures, etc.)
   - Family-naming patterns (patronymic suffixes, locative attribution)
   - Gender marking (where applicable to the source culture)

5. Generator surface:
   wyrd kenning-person <culture> [--gender] [--with-backstory]
   Output: name + (optional) etymology + (optional) 2-3 sentence backstory consistent with the named culture's lore.

6. Schema additions:
   - personal_name etymon class (or use a tag distinguishing personal-name morphemes from place-name morphemes)
   - naming_system table linking morphemes to their cluster
   - cluster sensitivity_level column (bundled / framework-only / requires-review)

Acceptance criteria:
- For each non-restricted cluster, the generator produces credible new names that read as belonging to the same culture as the seed sample.
- For restricted clusters, the generator returns a clear 'framework only' message + a guide to plugging in community-supplied data.
- A regression test: 'Sakuachi-style generator produces Sakuachi-shape names; the same generator never produces Greek-style names; vice versa for the Greek generator'.

Soft prereqs: Schema flags ticket (wyrd-yan), Wiktionary mining (wyrd-4rt). Independent of the place-name authoring work.

Out of scope:
- Full character-sheet generation (stat blocks, equipment) — the kenning-person generator outputs name + backstory, no game stats.
notes:
Scope discipline (2026-05-01, per user, mirrors wyrd-0ab): only ingest etymology entries when complete and useful. Stage the rest.

v1 SCOPE CUTS for personal-name etymology:
- Real-language proper-name clusters (Greek-style, OE/ON heroic, Italian, Slavic): bundle and mine — Wiktionary + Behind-the-Name cover these well.
- Pseudo-real-language clusters (PF's pseudo-Greek, pseudo-Norse): author productive rules ONLY when the rule set is grounded in clearly-sourced components.
- Active-community-coded clusters (Erutaki/Inuit, Mwangi/Bantu, Tian/Chinese): D7 framework only. Don't bundle; provide the slot.
- Pure-invention clusters (Vornen, Dronuk, Inizkar — single-name occurrences with no real-world analog): SKIP for v1. Defer to a future pass.

Same etymology-completeness gate as wyrd-0ab applies. Names that don't pass go to pending_etymology staging, not the live etymon table. Generator never sees staged entries.

Cluster-level v1 success metric: how many CULTURE-CLUSTERS unlock generation, not how many individual names. A bundled Greek-style cluster (with productive rules) is more valuable than 50 invented one-off names.

title: Wiktionary etymology mining: ingester, enrichment bridges, and corpus expansion
description:
Why this exists:

The current pipeline mines scholarly etymology BOOKS (Mawer, Skeat, Joyce, etc.) which are place-name-specialized. There is no general-etymology lookup layer in the lexicon. For:

- wyrd-98f: authoring etymons for unaccounted fragments like 'great', 'broad', 'court', 'long' (modern English content words),
- wyrd-ami: cross-validating Bosworth-Toller and Cleasby-Vigfusson mining against Wiktionary's structured cognate trees,
- wyrd-0ab: looking up the real-world etymology bucket (Bucket A) for fantasy names that turn out to be borrowings,

we need a free, broad, mineable etymology source. Wiktionary etymology sections are CC-BY-SA, mineable via the dump, and frequently deeper than commercial single-paragraph references.

What needs to be done:

1. Pipeline: download Wiktionary dump (or use Tatu Ylonen's wiktextract pre-parsed JSON, which is the canonical clean version). Filter to entries with a non-empty Etymology section.

2. Parser: read wiktextract's JSON output. Each entry yields:
   - canonical_form (the headword)
   - language (English, Old English, Old Norse, Greek, etc.)
   - etymology_text (free-form prose)
   - etymology_templates (parsed: {{inh|en|ang|brycg}} = inherited from OE 'brycg', {{cog|on|brú}} = cognate to ON 'brú', etc.)
   - first_attestation_date (when present)
   - PoS, glosses

3. Ingestion: synthetic source row id='wiktionary-en' (and per major language). Each Wiktionary entry becomes etymon rows with citations to the synthetic source. Etymology_templates feed lemma_id linkage when the inheritance/cognate target is already in the lexicon.

4. Use cases:
   - wyrd-98f integration: when the unaccounted miner hits 'court', the authoring pass first looks up Wiktionary; if a clear etymology is present, ingest from there with confidence='high'. Falls back to LLM-generative only if Wiktionary doesn't cover it.
   - Cross-validation for wyrd-ami: bosworth_toller_oe entry for 'wyrm' should correspond to a Wiktionary entry; if the two disagree, flag for manual review.
   - Bucket A classification for wyrd-0ab: 'troll' lookup → Wiktionary returns ON etymology → fantasy creature 'troll' resolves to canonical etymology, not constructed.

5. License attribution: Wiktionary is CC-BY-SA. Each ingested row's notes field carries the attribution string ('via Wiktionary, CC-BY-SA, accessed YYYY-MM'). The exported meanings.json bundle ships with a NOTICE file stating the Wiktionary attribution.

6. Idempotent re-mining: as Wiktionary updates, re-running the import should update existing rows in place (UPSERT on (canonical_form, language, source_id='wiktionary-en')).

Acceptance criteria:
- 50K+ etymon rows ingested from a fresh Wiktionary dump.
- Cross-coverage check: random sample of 100 existing rando-port etymons should have non-zero Wiktionary cite count.
- A test that exercises wyrd-98f's path through Wiktionary lookup before falling back to LLM generation.

title: Constructed-etymology pipeline: post-hoc credible histories for fantasy bestiary content
description:
Why this exists:

Take an existing fantasy creature/place/NPC name (e.g. from pfsrd2-data, OGL-licensed) and synthesize a credible etymology that follows real linguistic patterns — sound shifts, productive composition rules, plausible PIE/Greek/Latin/PGmc roots. Output: each fantasy name gets a worked-out morpheme decomposition + hypothetical attestation chain + modern reflex, marked clearly as constructed-etymology so the realistic pipeline never touches it.

This turns the project from a name generator into a worldbuilding consistency tool. A GM picks 'sahuagin coast culture, Norse-coded geography' — the engine produces Trollbúðir-shape place names AND retro-fits credible Norse etymology onto the sahuagin canon so the linguistic substrate hangs together.

What needs to be done:

1. Bucket classifier: for each fantasy name, identify the etymology bucket via LLM:
   - Bucket A — Real etymology: name borrowed from a real language with traceable roots (troll, goblin, dragon, sphinx, manticore). Resolves to canonical etymon via Wiktionary mining.
   - Bucket B — Constructed-but-rule-legal: name is invented but transparently follows linguistic patterns (Drakainia from Greek δράκαινα; Hippogriff from Greek ἵππος + γρύψ). Etymology is post-hoc analyzable; mark constructed_etymology=TRUE.
   - Bucket C — Pure invention: name has no traceable pattern (Kashrishi). Generate plausible PIE/Greek/Sanskrit roots that *would* yield this surface form under known sound shifts; mark constructed_etymology=TRUE with a 'pure-invention' notes flag.

2. Authoring CLI: `wyrd kenning lexicon mine-bestiary <pfsrd2-data-path> --provider anthropic --apply`
   - For each name, run bucket-classifier + appropriate authoring path.
   - For Bucket A: use Wiktionary lookup; output a normal etymon row.
   - For Bucket B: LLM generates morpheme breakdown + cited Greek/Latin/etc. roots; validates via 'apparent roots must match a known etymon in the source language'.
   - For Bucket C: LLM proposes PIE roots + sound-shift chain to surface form; result marked low confidence + pure-invention.

3. Worked attestation chain (optional pass): for each accepted constructed etymology, generate a hypothetical Domesday-style attestation chain showing how the modern form would have evolved (1086 *Ulberetona* ← OE *Ūleberatūn*). Stored in toponym_attestation with source='constructed-history:<creature>' so the real attestation table isn't polluted.

4. Worldbuilding mode in the generator: GM specifies (geography-coding, creature-pool, register-tags). Generator pulls from the constructed-etymon pool with the appropriate semantic+language tags.

5. Test cases that should work end-to-end:
   - Mind Flayer → OE *myndflēre* (mynd + flēre, real roots) → ModE Mindflearston via -tūn suffix.
   - Rust Monster → OE *rūst-aglǽca* (rust + ancient-fierce-one) → place-name reflex.
   - Owlbear → OE *ūlebera* (ūle + bera, real roots) → ModE Owlberton.

OGL/CUP note: pfsrd2-data is OGL/Paizo CUP licensed; derived etymology corpus stays under that umbrella. User confirmed they work in OGL space and PF Patreon-tier monetization is allowed.

Acceptance criteria:
- For 50 sample creature names, 80%+ get a coherent bucket assignment.
- For Bucket A creatures, etymology entries cite real Wiktionary references.
- For Bucket B, post-hoc analyzable roots are present and plausible to a linguist.
- For Bucket C, proposed PIE roots generate the surface form via known sound shifts (verifiable by re-running the forward derivation).
- Worldbuilding-mode generator produces names that mix realistic toponym morphology with the fantasy bestiary's etymological substrate consistently.

Soft prereqs: Schema flags ticket; Fantasy register expansion epic (shares schema, complementary work).
notes:
Scope discipline (2026-05-01, per user): the lexicon must not be diluted by thin or guessed etymologies. Bucket assignment != ingest-worthy.

v1 SCOPE CUT: drop Bucket C (pure invention) entirely. PIE-shape root guesses for names like Vloriak/Dronuk/Inizkar would compete with scholar-cited morphemes in the lexicon at equal weight; that dilutes generation quality. Defer to a future pass when more root words exist.

v1 BUCKET B GATE: only author when EVERY morpheme has a clearly sourced, productive component. If even one root is a guess, skip and stage. Examples that pass:
- Mind Flayer = OE mynd + flēre (both real OE, attested)
- Tatzlwyrm = Ger Tatze (paw) + OE wyrm (both real, productive in compounds)
- Owlbear = OE ūle + bera (both real OE)

v1 BUCKET A: primary path. Real-language borrowings via Wiktionary lookup. Probably 30–50% of bestiary clears.

Etymology-completeness gate (REQUIRED before ingest):
1. canonical form
2. all roots present and Wiktionary-cite-able OR scholar-cite-able
3. at least one gloss
4. language attribution per morpheme
5. sound-shift derivation worked through (not 'roughly')
6. at least one productive reflex pattern (place-name-suffix-compatible)

Anything failing the gate -> pending_etymology STAGING table, NOT etymon. Re-evaluable on each new mining batch as the root inventory grows. Schema add: pending_etymology(id, candidate_name, source_id, proposed_breakdown_json, missing_pieces_json, last_evaluated, blocked_by_etymon_ids).

Acceptance criteria revision:
- Of bestiary names processed, ingested-fraction is whatever passes the gate (probably 20-40% v1; user is fine with this).
- Of staged names, the staging table is auditable and re-runnable.
- Generator never sees pending_etymology rows.
- A test confirms: 'an etymology with one guessed root is staged, not ingested'.

title: Fantasy register expansion via PD OE/ON dictionary mining (wyrm/troll/draca/jǫtunn)
description:
Why this exists:

Lots of OE and ON words have valid place-name-shape semantics (creature names, weapons, terrain features, descriptive adjectives, religious/sacred terms) but never made it into attested toponyms by historical accident. wyrm (dragon), troll, draca, þyrs (giant), jǫtunn, ælf, dreki, vargr, draugr, ormr — perfectly legal morphemes the place-name corpus simply didn't use.

Adding these unlocks a fantasy register that's *credibly British* — Trollburg sounds right because it's a rule-legal ON+OE compound (`troll + burh`), not because we coded ON as 'monstrous'. D6's morally-neutral-palette architecture works exactly here: morphemes carry semantic tags (creature, supernatural, grim), and the fantasy generator filters on tags, not language.

What needs to be done:

1. Mine PD OE dictionary: Bosworth-Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary (Bosworth 1898 + Toller 1921 supplement). Free at archive.org; clean text via bosworthtoller.com or wiktextract. ~30K entries.
   - Filter to entries with semantic class compatible with toponym formation (nouns, productive adjectives).
   - Per-entry: extract canonical form, gloss(es), part-of-speech, mark as attested_realworld=TRUE, attested_in_toponyms refresh-via-trigger.
   - Synthetic source row: bosworth_toller_oe.

2. Mine PD ON dictionary: Cleasby-Vigfusson Icelandic-English Dictionary (1874). Free at archive.org. Same workflow.
   - Synthetic source: cleasby_vigfusson_on.

3. Tag entries with semantic class via LLM pass. Tags drawn from a curated vocabulary: creature, supernatural, grim, mystical, weapon, plant, terrain, descriptive, religious, mortuary, social-rank, animal-domestic, animal-wild, etc. Use Haiku (cheap, accurate-enough for tag classification).

4. Refresh the attested_in_toponyms boolean: any etymon that appears in toponym_etymology_element is TRUE; everything else is FALSE.

5. Generator surface: --fantasy or --include-unattested flag opens up attested_realworld=TRUE + attested_in_toponyms=FALSE etymons. Composes with existing -tūn / -hām / -burh / -lēah / -ford suffixes via existing rules.

6. Validation: produce sample fantasy-mode names per culture and eyeball. Trollburg-shape names should fall out naturally with --grim --mystical filters.

Acceptance criteria:
- Bosworth-Toller mining produces 5K+ new etymon rows with semantic-class tags.
- Cleasby-Vigfusson mining produces 1K+ ON etymon rows.
- Generator with --fantasy --grim produces names like Wyrmwick, Trollburg, Drakefell, Wraithford, Þyrsleah at reasonable frequency.
- Default (non-fantasy) generation is unchanged — no unattested forms leak into realistic output.
- A regression test: 'realistic mode never produces a name containing a etymon with attested_in_toponyms=FALSE'.

Soft prereq: Schema flags ticket (attested_realworld / attested_in_toponyms / constructed_etymology columns).
notes:
Scope refinement after spot-check against current lexicon (2026-05-01):

Many of the well-known fantasy-relevant morphemes are ALREADY in the rando-port seed with appropriate semantic tags:
- wyrm (OE) — tagged magic, monster, reptile
- elf (OE) — tagged magic, monster
- thyrs (OE giant) — tagged monster
- ūle (OE owl), wulf (OE) — properly classed

So the scope of this ticket is more 'fill the long tail of fantasy-register morphemes' than 'build the inventory from scratch'. The high-leverage gaps are ON-side (troll, jǫtunn, vargr, draugr, dreki) and the OE long tail (draca, grendel, nicor, heolstor, bera, niðr).

Practical implication: this ticket can probably be done in two passes — a small targeted manual pass for the ~20 named-fantasy-morpheme gaps that have obvious productivity (a day's work), and the broader Bosworth-Toller / Cleasby-Vigfusson dump-mining as a separate follow-up for completeness. The targeted pass alone unlocks 80% of the fantasy generation value.

title: Add 'fiction' tag as realistic-vs-fantasy generator gate
description:
Why this exists:

Several upcoming work tracks need to mark etymons by their relationship to historical reality:
- 'OE word that exists in dictionaries but never showed up in attested toponyms' (real lexicon, just unattested in toponyms specifically)
- 'Greek-shaped invention that postdates classical Greek' (constructed etymology applied to fantasy content)
- 'Pure invention with no linguistic ancestor' (post-hoc analyzed for shape)

These categories need to coexist with the existing scholar-cited morphemes without polluting the consensus / promotion framework. The realistic generator must NEVER draw from non-attested forms; the fantasy generator opts in via tag filter.

What needs to be done:

Add three boolean columns on `etymon`:

- `attested_realworld` (default TRUE): the word exists in real-world historical record (Bosworth-Toller has it, Cleasby-Vigfusson has it, etc.). FALSE means the morpheme is constructed for fantasy use.
- `attested_in_toponyms` (default FALSE, set TRUE by trigger / refresh query when any toponym_etymology_element references the etymon): word has appeared in at least one attested toponym.
- `constructed_etymology` (default FALSE): the etymology breakdown is post-hoc / fanfic etymology applied to a fantasy creature/place name, not an actual historical derivation. When TRUE, the row's source_id should point at a synthetic constructed-etymology source.

Promotion rule update:
- `etymon_consensus` view's >=3-witness promotion only counts witnesses where attested_realworld=TRUE and constructed_etymology=FALSE. Otherwise unattested forms could 'promote' via duplicated bestiary entries.

Generator filter update:
- Default mode: only draw from etymons where attested_realworld=TRUE AND attested_in_toponyms=TRUE. Pure-realistic.
- --fantasy or --include-unattested: allow attested_realworld=TRUE AND attested_in_toponyms=FALSE. (Real OE word, never historically used in toponym, but rule-legal.)
- --constructed: also allow constructed_etymology=TRUE etymons, gated by tag filter (--grim, --mystical, etc.).

Acceptance criteria:
- Migration script adds the columns with the documented defaults.
- A query that lists 'etymons available for realistic generation' returns only attested_realworld=TRUE AND attested_in_toponyms=TRUE rows.
- A populate query sets attested_in_toponyms=TRUE for every etymon currently referenced by toponym_etymology_element.
- The existing meanings.json export filters to only include realistic-mode etymons by default; fantasy variants ship as a separate bundle.
notes:
Refinement (2026-05-01, per user): use a TAG, not boolean columns, as the gate.

The 'fiction' tag (or similar — 'fictional', 'non-historical') is the realistic-vs-fantasy gate. Reasons:
- etymon_tag table already exists, no schema migration
- composes with existing D6 tag-filter machinery (--harsh, --grim) on the same surface
- content classification belongs in tags; metadata belongs in columns
- nests cleanly with sub-tags (pf2-bestiary, constructed-germanic, etc.)

Revised scope:

(1) Add the 'fiction' tag value to the canonical tag vocabulary, documented as the realistic/fantasy gate.

(2) Default generator behavior: filter draws to exclude 'fiction'-tagged etymons unless the user opts in. CLI flag like --include-fiction, or default-on a tag-include for 'fiction' in fantasy mode.

(3) Other tags that nest under 'fiction':
- pf2-bestiary (creature etymons from wyrd-0ab)
- pf2-npc (personal-name etymons from wyrd-kjc)
- constructed-<language> (Greek/Norse/Latin-shape but fictional, e.g. constructed-greek)
- pure-invention (Bucket C; deferred per user but tag exists for staging)

(4) attested_in_toponyms — KEEP as derived data, NOT a column. A refresh script tags every etymon referenced by toponym_etymology_element with 'toponym-attested'. The generator's realistic mode prefers (but doesn't require) this tag for higher-quality draws.

(5) constructed_etymology — drop from schema. Replace with the 'constructed-<language>' tag chain.

Acceptance criteria:
- 'fiction' tag added to the tag vocabulary doc
- Generator filter implements --no-tag fiction as default for realistic mode (or whatever the equivalent is in the existing flag-set)
- A regression test: a fiction-tagged etymon (test fixture) does NOT appear in default-mode generated names; does appear under --include-fiction
- A query that lists all etymons available for realistic generation excludes fiction-tagged entries

This subsumes the original three-column proposal and is much cleaner. The user is right that this is the natural primitive.

title: Trie-based morpheme matcher: replace iterate-all-morphemes with segmentation DAG
description:
Why this exists:

The current matcher (Name.find_meaning, ported from Rando) iterates over every morpheme in the meanings DB and tries each as a pre/post/inner/free match against the name. For 10K toponyms × 1500 morphemes that's ~15M lookups per corpus pass. Plus 'find all decompositions' (which wyrd-08m needs) is awkward because the matcher's data flow is morpheme-first, not position-first.

A trie is the right structure for both problems:

(1) Performance: walking a name through a trie is O(name_length) per name, finding ALL matches at all positions in one pass. ~200x speedup on routine corpus passes.

(2) Multi-decomposition: every accepting state in the trie marks a morpheme boundary. Every full path through the resulting segmentation DAG is a decomposition. Enumerating all valid decompositions is a graph traversal, not a heuristic enumeration with reduce=False + dedupe-by-signature.

(3) Inflection: if inflected variants are inserted directly into the trie (each pointing at its lemma_id + inflection tag), inflection resolution happens at match time for free. wyrd-lx8's 'inflection-strip preprocessing' option becomes unnecessary; option (b) of that ticket (expanded variants) becomes the natural design.

What needs to be done:

1. Build two tries keyed by canonical_form:
   - Forward (left-to-right) for pre/free/inner-position morphemes scanning forward from each position.
   - Reverse (right-to-left) for post/inner morphemes scanning backward from each position.
   - Each accepting state stores: etymon_id, lemma_id, inflection (or null), language, position_pref.

2. Match algorithm per toponym:
   - For each position i in 0..len(name): walk the forward trie from name[i:] to find all morphemes that start at i. Similarly the reverse trie.
   - Build a position-graph: nodes are positions in the name, edges are morpheme matches connecting position i to position i+morpheme_length.
   - Enumerate all paths from position 0 to position len(name) — each path is a decomposition. Unaccounted fragments are the gaps between matched edges.

3. Quality scoring (feeds wyrd-08m's canonical picker):
   - Sum of unaccounted-fragment characters
   - Total morpheme count (Occam preference)
   - Lemma-confidence (sum of witness counts for matched lemmas — D4 consensus)
   - Position-preference adherence (penalize a 'post' morpheme appearing as 'pre')

4. API surface mirroring Name.find_meaning:
   - all_decompositions(name) -> list[Decomposition]
   - canonical_decomposition(name) -> Decomposition (uses scoring; ties go to scholarly attribution if available — see wyrd-08m)
   - plus a stable signature() per decomposition for cache keys (matches wyrd-cv3's toponym_decomposition row identity)

5. Build incrementally vs full rebuild:
   - First implementation can rebuild on every load.
   - Persistent serialization (pickle / sqlite trie table) is a future optimization once the rebuild cost shows up.

Acceptance criteria:
- For every toponym in the existing corpus, the trie matcher produces a superset of decompositions equivalent to the current Name.find_meaning(reduce=False) output (modulo dedupe).
- A regression test asserts that the canonical decomposition for a known set of scholarly-attested toponyms matches the scholar's breakdown.
- Performance: a full corpus decompose pass (10K toponyms) runs in seconds, not minutes.
- The Braitham Gate regression test (a descriptive+topography first-word compound; user's favorite) still surfaces as a valid decomposition.

Soft prereq: none — this can land standalone with the existing meanings.json data model. wyrd-cv3 (corpus DB ingest) and wyrd-08m (multiplicity schema) become much easier to implement on top of this engine. wyrd-lx8 (inflection-aware) is naturally subsumed by (3) above if inflected variants are present in the trie source data.

Notes:
- The trie should be language-aware: position_pref is set per (etymon, language) and must be respected during matching.
- Edge case: very short morphemes (2 chars) cause combinatorial explosion in the segmentation DAG. Add a min-length threshold or require non-overlapping at scoring time.

title: Decomposition multiplicity: store competing breakdowns + canonical-decomposition picker aligned with scholarship
description:
Why this exists:

The matcher (Name.find_meaning with reduce=False) returns every plausible morpheme breakdown for a toponym. With reduce=True it picks one via heuristic. Two failure modes follow:

(1) FALSE GAPS: fragment X shows as unaccounted under decomposition A, but under decomposition B every fragment is accounted. If A got cached/picked, X looks like a gap when it isn't. The unaccounted miner would then waste authoring effort on X.

(2) FALSE HITS: morpheme M is counted as 'matched' because it's a substring under decomposition A, but the scholarly decomposition B doesn't use M at all. M's apparent corpus frequency is inflated.

Real example shape: 'Stratford' could decompose as:
  A: Strat + ford (street-ford — scholarly)
  B: Strat + for + d (spurious overlap with -d ending or rare 'for' morpheme)
  C: Stratfor + d
The picker has to consistently favor A.

What needs to be done:

1. Schema (extends wyrd-cv3): toponym_decomposition is one row per (toponym, decomposition_signature). Many rows per toponym allowed. Columns include:
   - decomposition_signature (canonical hash of (morpheme_ids, unaccounted_strings) ordered)
   - morpheme_ids (JSON list / normalized table — TBD)
   - unaccounted_fragments (JSON list)
   - quality_score (number of unaccounted, total morpheme count, lemma-confidence)
   - is_canonical BOOLEAN (true for at most one per toponym)
   - canonical_source ('scholar' | 'unique-zero-unacc' | 'tiebreaker' | NULL)

2. Canonical picker (priority order):
   a. Scholar match: a decomposition whose morpheme set matches an existing toponym_etymology row's elements is canonical.
   b. Unique zero-unaccounted: if exactly ONE breakdown has zero unaccounted, it's canonical.
   c. Tiebreaker for multi-zero-unaccounted cases:
      - Prefer fewer total morphemes (Occam)
      - Prefer breakdowns using lemmas with higher witness counts (D4 consensus signal)
      - Prefer breakdowns avoiding very rare morphemes
      - Stable lex-order final tiebreak so the choice is deterministic

3. Honest gap counting: a fragment is 'unaccounted' for a toponym only if it appears in the canonical decomposition's unaccounted_fragments. Fragments that disappear under any zero-unaccounted decomposition don't count.

4. Honest hit counting: a morpheme is 'matched' for a toponym only if it appears in the canonical decomposition's morpheme_ids. Substring co-occurrences in non-canonical decompositions don't count.

5. CLI surfacing: wyrd kenning lexicon decompose --apply both stores the multiplicity rows AND picks the canonical via the rules above. Re-run after authoring lifts (mining adds new etymons that may unlock new decompositions; canonical picks may shift; quality scores recompute).

Acceptance criteria:
- Toponyms with scholarly attribution have their canonical decomposition aligned with the scholar's breakdown.
- Toponyms with multiple zero-unaccounted decompositions get a deterministic canonical via tiebreakers (test fixture).
- Re-running the decompose step after authoring is idempotent on canonical selection (no churn from arbitrary tiebreaks).
- Coverage and gap reports use canonical-only counts.

Notes:
- Touches Name.find_meaning's downstream consumers (rebuild-proportions, unaccounted, explainer). Explainer can keep showing all alternatives — it should — but mark canonical visually.
- The 'quality score' is a placeholder; concrete formula is a design call during implementation. Document it in DECISIONS.md when settled (proposed D21).
notes:
Real-world framing: decomposition multiplicity is NOT just an engineering quirk — place name etymologies are genuinely ambiguous in scholarship. Schema's toponym_etymology table is intentionally one-to-many because 'multiple breakdowns per toponym are expected and welcomed: they encode disagreement, which is information' (lexicon.sql comment).

The canonical picker should mirror this:
- Toponym with ONE scholarly breakdown → that breakdown is canonical.
- Toponym with MULTIPLE scholarly breakdowns → all are canonical-ish (no single 'truth' in this case; tag the rows as 'scholar-disagreement').
- Toponym with NO scholarly breakdown → matcher's heuristic pick is 'best-guess', not canonical-truth.

Honest gap counting then becomes:
A fragment is 'unaccounted' for a toponym only if EVERY valid decomposition (all scholarly + best-guess) leaves it unaccounted. If ANY breakdown resolves it, the fragment isn't a real gap there.

Honest hit counting:
A morpheme is 'matched' for a toponym only if it appears in AT LEAST ONE canonical breakdown. If a morpheme only appears via spurious overlap in non-canonical heuristic decompositions, it doesn't count.

This is more permissive than 'pick exactly one canonical' — and that's the point. The schema gets to express scholarly disagreement instead of papering over it.

title: Ingest bulk place_names corpora into lexicon DB for query-able winnowing
description:
Why this exists:

Today the bulk toponym corpus lives in data/{english,scottish,welsh,irish}_place_names.json (~10K names total). The matcher reads it at runtime to compute proportions. The lexicon DB's toponym table has only the few-thousand scholar-cited names from mining (toponyms with formal etymology breakdowns).

Several authoring/triage workflows want to run analytic queries over the FULL corpus joined with mining output — finding which corpus names have scholarly attribution, which corpus toponyms contribute each gap fragment (cross-link with wyrd-bvp), coverage delta per mining run, etc. Today these require ad-hoc Python scripts that re-decompose JSON each time. Ingesting the bulk corpus makes them straightforward joins.

What needs to be done:

1. Populate toponym table from the per-culture JSONs, with synthetic source rows:
   - source.id = 'place-names-corpus-english' / -scottish / -welsh / -irish
   - source.notes captures provenance ('User-curated bulk toponym list, runtime stats source')
   - Each name becomes a toponym row with country/region from the JSON structure
   - Use existing UNIQUE (modern_name, country, region) index — re-running the populate is idempotent

2. Cache decomposition output per toponym so we don't re-run the matcher every time:
   - new table toponym_decomposition (toponym_id, source='matcher-vN', json_blob | normalized rows)
   - stores: morphemes matched, unaccounted fragments, decomposition signature, perfect-decompose boolean
   - matcher version stamped so re-running with an updated meanings DB writes a new version
   - rebuild-proportions can read from this table directly

3. CLI: `wyrd kenning lexicon ingest-place-names` (one-shot populate) + `wyrd kenning lexicon decompose --culture english --apply` (cache decompositions per-toponym)

4. Update unaccounted (wyrd-bvp work) to read from toponym + toponym_decomposition instead of re-running the matcher on JSON.

Soft prereq: wyrd-lx8 (inflection-aware matcher) — otherwise cached decompositions inherit the inflated-gap problem. Feasible to do in either order; if we ingest first, we just re-run the decompose step after lx8 lands.

Scope considerations:

- Schema change is small but changes a load-bearing column semantic on `toponym` (was 'scholar-cited'; becomes 'any toponym we care about'). Add a query-able status column ('corpus-only' / 'scholar-attested') so analyses can filter cleanly.
- Total row growth: ~10K toponyms + ~10K decompositions. Negligible.
- meanings.json + the runtime path stay unchanged (D1) — this is purely an authoring-side enhancement.

Acceptance criteria:
- `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM toponym` after populate ≈ sum of per-culture name counts
- `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM toponym_decomposition WHERE NOT perfect_decompose` matches the count of gap-fragment contributors
- A query that lists corpus toponyms by gap-fragment count returns sensible results within a second on the full corpus

title: unaccounted: surface scholarly-corpus presence for each gap fragment
description:
Why this exists:

When the unaccounted miner reports a fragment like 'court' (frequency=27 in english toponyms), we don't currently know whether scholars have written about it. The fragment might:

- Appear in 5 scholarly books with consistent etymological context → strong signal it's a known place-name term, just not in our lexicon yet
- Appear in 0 books → modern coinage, OCR garbage, or coincidental
- Appear in 1 book in a clear etymology context → we have a candidate scholarly citation we can attach when we author the etymon

Right now this evidence is reachable manually (grep through sources/*.txt) but the gap-triage workflow doesn't surface it automatically. Adding it would let us point each gap fragment at potentially-useful data and accelerate the authoring step.

What needs to be done:

Extend `wyrd kenning unaccounted` (or a sibling subcommand) so each fragment in the report is annotated with:

- count of distinct sources/*.txt files where the fragment appears (word-boundary match + OCR-tolerant)
- a 1-2 sample snippet per fragment with surrounding context (~80 chars)
- an indicator if the snippet looks like an etymology body (year + signal markers per _ENTRY_BODY_SIGNALS) vs. running prose

Output as JSON-with-evidence so the authoring loop can chain it directly:

```
{ "fragment": "court", "count": 27,
  "corpus_hits": 8,
  "strong_hits": 2,  // hits inside an etymology body
  "snippets": [
    {"source": "johnston_1915_...", "snippet": "...Court Henry. From Welsh cwrt 'court'...", "in_etym_body": true},
    ...
  ] }
```

Implementation reuses logic from reverse_search_attestations / lexicon.py:
- normalize_ocr_form on the body text
- regex word-boundary match
- cross-check with _ENTRY_BODY_SIGNALS to flag in-etymology hits

Acceptance criteria:
- New subcommand `wyrd kenning lexicon corpus-evidence <fragment>` (or extension of `unaccounted --with-evidence`) produces the annotated JSON.
- A test case where a known fragment ('court' or 'great') has expected non-zero corpus hits in our existing scholarly source corpus.
- Documented in INGESTION.md as the recommended triage pre-step before authoring etymologies for top-N fragments.

title: Mine place_names corpora for missing morphemes and ingest etymologies
description:
Why this exists:

Place names that don't fully decompose against meanings.json leave behind unaccounted fragments — modern English content words ("great", "broad", "long", "new"), Norman-French-loan place vocab ("court", "manor"), specialized topographic terms, and so on. Per the user's recall, ~78% of place name fragments are unaccounted. After the inflectional fix (see blocker), the real gap list will sharpen, and a meaningful share of it will be modern-English words with well-trodden etymologies that we should be able to author and ingest.

What needs to be done:

1. Run `wyrd kenning unaccounted` per culture (english, scottish, welsh, irish), produce ranked top-50 fragment lists.

2. Triage the lists into buckets:
   - Modern English with well-known etymology (LLM-generative bucket — "great", "long", "new", "hill", "green")
   - Specialized place-name vocab requiring scholarship (manual / book-mining first — "holm", "shaw", "ley")
   - OCR garbage / alt spellings of known morphemes (cluster cleanup via fuzzy-search)

3. Build an authoring pipeline for the LLM-generative bucket:
   - Synthetic source row, e.g. `english-fragment-mining` (separate from `rando-port`), so provenance stays auditable
   - LLM-generative extraction for one fragment at a time. NO form-in-body validator (there is no body) — instead, validate by requiring the LLM to provide a published-dictionary gloss or a Latin/Greek root reference; reject if it can't
   - Mark all rows confidence=low until corroborated by a scholarly source
   - CLI: `wyrd kenning lexicon mine-fragments english --top 50 --provider anthropic --review`

4. Ingest, run the post-mining chain (link-lemmas, normalize-ocr, reverse-search, fuzzy-search), report on coverage delta.

5. Iterate per culture.

Tier choice: per D19, Sonnet is reserved for runtime user features. But for *generative* etymology authoring (no source to validate against), the cost-vs-quality calculus differs from extraction mining — Sonnet's reduced over-extrapolation under guidance might pay off. Worth comparing Haiku vs Sonnet on a small sample.

Out of scope here:
- Historical sound-shift modeling for register/era axes (D5). Different machinery (phonology rule chains over morphemes), worth its own epic.

Acceptance criteria:
- Each culture's top-20 modern-English-bucket fragments are ingested with low-confidence rows tagged to a synthetic source.
- Post-ingestion run of `wyrd kenning unaccounted english` shows the ingested fragments no longer in the top-50.
- decompose-rate (perfect / total names) per culture lifts measurably.

title: unaccounted matcher: resolve inflected variants to their lemma before reporting gaps
description:
Why this exists:

Currently `wyrd kenning unaccounted` decomposes place names against meanings.json (lemma-only, rando-port seed format). Toponyms contain inflected forms — OE genitives (`cotes`), datives (`cotum`), weak obliques (`cotan`), nominative -u (`denu`, `wudu`), and plurals. Without inflection awareness, those forms appear in the gap list as "unaccounted" even though their lemma is in the seed. Result: the ~78% gap rate the user remembers is inflated by inflectional variants of known morphemes.

The lexicon DB already has lemma_id + inflection self-FK on etymon (D8). What's missing is using it on the matcher side.

What needs to be done:

Three plausible paths, pick one (or hybrid):

(a) Lexicon-aware matcher path: route the unaccounted tool through the lexicon DB (etymon_consensus or etymon_lemma view), so inflected variants resolve to their lemma and don't show as gaps. Pro: highest quality. Con: couples the tool to the authoring DB (tension with D1 which keeps runtime decoupled). The unaccounted CLI is authoring-side though, so this tension is mild.

(b) Expanded meanings.json path: when exporting meanings.json from the lexicon, expand each lemma row to all its known inflected forms. Runtime stays simple — the matcher's existing meanings.json lookup natively matches inflected forms because they're in the file. Pro: keeps runtime decoupled. Con: meanings.json grows; need to teach the export step about lemma rollup.

(c) Inflection-strip preprocessing path: before classifying a fragment as unaccounted, try common OE/ME inflection-strip rules (-s, -es, -en, -an, -um, -es genitive). Pro: no data-layer changes. Con: prior session removed an over-stripping rule (-u was eating real lemmas like wudu, denu) so the rule list is conservative-by-default.

Recommend hybrid: (b) covers the well-attested inflections we have data for; (c) is a small fallback for the long tail.

Acceptance criteria:
- After fix, `wyrd kenning unaccounted english data/english_place_names.json --top 50` returns a list dominated by genuine gaps (modern English content words, place-name-specific vocab) rather than inflected variants of seed morphemes.
- A regression test exercising at least one OE-inflected toponym fragment that resolves correctly post-fix.
- No regression on the existing inflection-strip rule denylist (wudu, denu must still be lemmas, not stripped to wud, den).

title: Export step: regenerate meanings.json from the lexicon DB
description:
DECISIONS.md D1 commits to keeping the runtime on data/meanings.json while the lexicon SQLite DB serves as the authoring-side store (mining, citation tracking, consensus, lemma linkage). The decision says 'a future export step (filed) will regenerate meanings.json from the lexicon when we want changes to ship.' That export step is not actually filed anywhere I can find — no ticket, no script, no module. This issue covers building it.

Scope:
- A CLI command (likely 'wyrd kenning export-meanings' or similar) that walks the lexicon DB, applies the promotion criteria, and writes a fresh meanings.json + the four <culture>_proportions.json files used by the runtime.
- Promotion criteria per D4: include etymons with N>=3 distinct scholar-witness citations and no breakdown disagreement. Etymons still standing on rando-port (Wikipedia seed) alone are included as legacy until corroborated.
- Per D14, hedged extractions (confidence='low') are exported but tagged so consumers can filter.
- Per D8, lemma+inflection linkage means we export the lemma's surface form with a side-table or inline note for inflected variants (whichever the runtime can consume without a refactor).
- Per D18, attested spelling variants (etymon_text_match.matched_form) ship alongside the canonical form so the generator can sample them — coordinate with wyrd-40m.
- Per D12, do NOT export search-evidence (etymon_text_match) as if it were citation evidence; only etymon_citation rolls up to consensus.

Acceptance:
- Re-running the export against the current lexicon produces a meanings.json that the existing kenning generator and KenningExplain explainer can load without changes.
- All existing tests still pass against the regenerated file.
- The exported file's morpheme count is >= the current bundled meanings.json (no regressions from the rando-port seed).
- Diff between regenerated and current bundled meanings.json is reviewable and surfaces the actual newly-promoted etymons.

Why this is load-bearing: every mining ticket (wyrd-yy3, wyrd-bzu, wyrd-gxf, wyrd-zga, wyrd-9w8, wyrd-3qq, wyrd-i88, wyrd-95f, the Mayan/Nahuatl ones, and wyrd-668) is currently queued behind this. Without the export, mining accrues to the lexicon but never reaches the user.

Inverse of seed_from_meanings; applies D4 promotion, rolls up D8 inflections + D22 OCR-losers, narrows per-reflex language arrays via reflex_etymon links. Bundled meanings.json unchanged (deliberate — user-driven swap).

title: Use attested spelling variants as randomizer targets in generation
description:
Per user observation: 19th-c scholars wrote 'denu' / 'dene' / 'denū' / 'dená' for the same OE word — spelling wasn't standardized. With the gloss-anchored fuzzy match work (etymon_text_match.matched_form), we now know each etymon's attested spelling variants across the corpus.

This is a generative feature, not just verification. When the kenning generator picks a morpheme, instead of always emitting the canonical form, it can RANDOMLY SAMPLE from the attested spellings:

  Pick etymon: 'denu' (OE valley)
  Attested variants: denu (8×), dene (12×), denū (3×), dená (1×)
  Sample weighted by attestation count → emit one of these in the output

Effect on output quality:
- Names feel pulled from real period documents instead of a database
- Different invocations produce stylistically varied output even with the same morpheme set
- For historical-mode generation (era=Old English), the variant feels more authentic
- For modern-mode generation, we use the canonical / modernized form

Implementation:
- Each etymon already has a canonical_form. The attested variants live in etymon_text_match.matched_form (after the fuzzy-search work).
- Add a function get_attested_variants(etymon_id) -> [(form, count), ...]
- Generation step that currently emits etymon.canonical_form → instead samples from variants weighted by count, with the canonical form having a baseline weight to ensure it shows up.
- A user-facing --variant-style flag: 'canonical' (current behavior, always canonical), 'attested' (sample from variants), 'random' (uniform over variants).

Pairs with wyrd-skm (period-aware) — different variants are more/less period-appropriate, and the generator should weight by period when emitting.
notes: Closed as duplicate of wyrd-q13 (D18 spelling variants), which shipped Meaning.pick_variant + Kenning --spelling-variety knob. The wyrd-40m description ('sample from etymon_text_match.matched_form weighted by attestation count, gated by --variant-style') describes exactly the same feature wyrd-q13's Meaning.pick_variant + --spelling-variety implements. Bundle export emits per-language _variants pools; runtime samples weighted by match_count.

title: Mine French place-name etymology corpora
description:
Per Claude-twin feedback. Standard reference is Dauzat's Dictionnaire étymologique des noms de lieux en France (not PD). PD options:

French as a fantasy register codes 'Norman noble', 'Frankish substrate', 'Gallo-Roman bones' — three strata corresponding to wyrd-{stratification} once that's filed. Mining these gives the morpheme inventory.

Pairs with the manorial-affix pattern (wyrd-{manorial}) — Norman family names extracted from this corpus + Domesday tenant lists make the conquest-layering generation viable.

title: Within-language stratum tagging (Brittonic/Latin/medieval/English in 'Welsh')
description:
Each major language palette has internal stratification we currently ignore:

- Welsh: Brittonic substrate + Latin layer (caer, pont, ffynnon — direct Latin loans) + native medieval Welsh + English borrowings + modern. A 'Welsh-flavored elven' generator pulling indiscriminately from all of it produces stylistic mush.
- French: Frankish substrate (-ville, -court, personal names in -hard / -old) + Gallo-Roman + medieval French + early modern + Occitan-influenced south.
- Old English: West Saxon vs Mercian vs Anglian dialect strata; pre-Christian vs Christian-influenced vocabulary.
- Old Norse: Eastern (Swedish/Danish) vs Western (Norwegian/Icelandic) traditions.

Schema addition: 'stratum' text column on etymon (or a separate etymon_stratum table for many-to-many — a morpheme can belong to multiple strata as it crosses periods).

Generation gains a --stratum filter:
  --style elven --stratum brittonic       → pre-Latin-influence Welsh-coded names
  --style elven --stratum medieval-welsh  → high-medieval flavor
  --style noble --stratum frankish        → 'pre-Gallo-Roman' French
  --style noble --stratum high-medieval   → standard chivalric French

Within-language stratum is the missing axis to sit alongside the cross-language wyrd-sfp work and the time-period wyrd-skm work.

title: Probabilistic morpheme co-occurrence learned from corpus
description:
Instead of hand-coding selectional restrictions on which morphemes combine with which (wyrd-{selection-restrictions}), build a co-occurrence matrix from the existing corpus and sample from the empirical distribution.

For each generic (-tun, -ham, -by, -worth, -ham, etc.), record the distribution of first-elements that ACTUALLY appear with it across attested toponyms, weighted by frequency.

Generation:
1. Pick a generic according to the language's structural pattern.
2. Sample a first-element from that generic's empirical co-occurrence distribution rather than uniformly from all etymons.

Wins:
- Catches implicit selectional restrictions WITHOUT having to hand-encode them.
- Surfaces regional patterns automatically (-thorpe concentrates with certain personal-name types in certain Yorkshire ridings; -by has a Danelaw signature; -wick fades after 1100). These show up in the matrix even if we never noticed them.
- Frequency-weighted: morphemes that are productive get used more, dead-ends get used less.
- Empirically grounded: the generator imitates real attested patterns rather than reasoning about them.

Implementation:
- New view or precomputed table: cooccurrence (first_etymon_id, second_etymon_id, count, weighted_count_by_period_and_region).
- Update NameGenerator.select() in proportions.py to consult cooccurrence stats when picking the second element given the first.
- Optional --no-cooccurrence flag for diagnostic comparison vs uniform sampling.

This basically obviates a large chunk of wyrd-{selection-restrictions} for free, and the test is concrete: generate 100 names with cooccurrence on, 100 with it off, eyeball both. The cooccurrence ones should read meaningfully more plausible.

Probably one of the highest-value tickets in the queue for output quality with little incremental work.
notes:
CORRECTION: marginal frequency-weighting is ALREADY in Rando (now wyrd) via proportions.py — usages and structures tables count how often each morpheme and each structural shape appears in real place names, and NameGenerator samples accordingly.

What's NOT in Rando is the CONDITIONAL joint distribution. The current generator samples each compound slot independently of the others — pick a -tun weighted by marginal -tun frequency, then independently pick a first-element by marginal frequency. There's no 'given that post-element is -tun, what's the distribution of typical pre-elements?'

The actual upgrade is adding the joint:
  P(first | second)
in addition to the existing marginal:
  P(first), P(second)

This catches the missing piece — that real corpora have strong selectional preferences (-tun pairs with personal-name and topographic prefixes; -ingaham pairs differently; -thorpe has Yorkshire personal-name regional bias). Independent sampling produces marginal-correct but joint-wrong combinations.

So this ticket is incremental on top of Rando's frequency-weighting, not a wholesale change. The data structure addition is one new precomputed table:
  cooccurrence (slot_a_etymon_id, slot_b_etymon_id, count)
The generation change is in proportions.py NameGenerator: sample slot 2 conditionally on slot 1 instead of independently. ~30 lines of Python.

Lower-effort than I initially framed it. Still high-value because joint vs marginal is what makes the difference between 'plausible morphology' and 'plausible attested name'.
REFINEMENT (per user, conversation): pure empirical co-occurrence has a known failure mode — it can only generate combinations that ALREADY appeared in the corpus. For a fantasy name generator we explicitly want NOVEL plausible names, not corpus retrieval.

Fix: Bayesian mixture model rather than pure empirical sampling.

  P(slot_b | slot_a) = α · P_empirical(slot_b | slot_a)        # attested co-occurrence
                     + β · P_class(slot_b | type(slot_a))       # selectional-type backoff
                     + γ · P_marginal(slot_b)                    # current Rando independent

with α + β + γ = 1.

Three regimes:
- α dominant: conservative, 'only attested combinations'. Good for testing, bad for generation.
- β dominant: feature-class backoff via selectional types (personal-name, topographic, ethnic-name, etc — same tags as wyrd-r8b). Generates NOVEL combinations within observed type patterns. Probably the sweet spot for fantasy-naming.
- γ dominant: reverts to current Rando behavior (independent marginals). Max novelty.

User-facing --novelty parameter lets a GM choose where to sit:
  --novelty conservative   → α=0.7, β=0.25, γ=0.05  (mostly attested)
  --novelty plausible      → α=0.3, β=0.55, γ=0.15  (default, type-driven novelty)
  --novelty wild           → α=0.1, β=0.3,  γ=0.6   (mostly marginal)

Smoothing: Laplace (add-1 to all pairs) or Kneser-Ney are standard NLP techniques, both short Python implementations. Required so unseen pairs get non-zero probability.

The β term depends on selectional types being tagged on etymons — that's wyrd-r8b. So sequence is:
  1. wyrd-r8b: tag etymons with selectional types (personal-name / topographic / etc.)
  2. wyrd-mj2 (this): build co-occurrence + class-level distributions
  3. Wire into NameGenerator with --novelty knob

Generation quality vs novelty becomes a tunable tradeoff, not a binary.
REFRAMED (per user): co-occurrence should operate on SEMANTIC CATEGORIES (tags), not morpheme IDs. The existing etymon_tag table already has these — plant, tree, water, religion, food, architecture, directional, male/female/saint name, etc.

Why semantic-class is the right level:

1. SPARSITY: ~30-50 tag classes vs ~2000 morpheme IDs. K×K matrix has ~1500 cells with hundreds of pairs each, vs N×N with most empty. The model actually fits the data.

2. GENERALIZATION: once we learn 'TREE + COLOR' pairs commonly, EVERY (oak, green) / (birch, white) / (ash, grey) is plausible whether attested or not. Solves the 'novel combinations from sparse data' problem.

3. CROSS-LANGUAGE: 'trees pair with greens' works in Welsh and Latin the same as in OE. wyrd-sfp (cross-cultural rendering) gets free transfer — semantic categories are language-neutral.

4. GM USABILITY: GM thinking 'forest village' picks (TREE + SETTLEMENT) tags; engine fills morphemes. Much better interface than picking morpheme IDs.

Revised generation flow:

  1. Pick structural pattern (1-word / 2-word / compound) — already in Rando.
  2. For each slot, sample a SEMANTIC CATEGORY using tag-level Bayesian
     conditional model:
       P(tag_b | tag_a) = α · P_empirical(tag_b | tag_a)
                        + β · P_marginal(tag_b)
     (Two-term mixture is sufficient at the tag level; the K×K matrix
     is dense enough that we don't need a third feature-backoff term.)
  3. For each picked category, sample a specific morpheme within that
     category, weighted by morpheme-marginal frequency PLUS stratum/
     period/region filters.
  4. Apply per-language mutation/sandhi (wyrd-q5v).

Morpheme-level conditional-frequency P(morpheme_b | morpheme_a) becomes a refinement, not the core. Most of the linguistic plausibility lives at the tag level.

Implementation: precompute a tag_cooccurrence table from existing toponym_etymology_element joins. Update NameGenerator.select() to do the two-stage sample. ~50 lines of Python plus a small precompute script.

Concrete next steps:
  1. wyrd-r8b (selectional types) is partially redundant now — modifier_tags already serve as semantic-type labels for most cases. Possibly close r8b in favor of fully leveraging existing tags.
  2. Build the tag_cooccurrence table.
  3. Wire two-stage sampling into NameGenerator.
  4. Generate 100 names with --novelty=plausible, eyeball, compare to current marginal-only sampling.
FITNESS TEST (per user, conversation): Rando produced 'Braitham Gate' — a felicitous novel name combining Brait- (size/broad) + -ham (habitative) + Gate (boundary/infrastructure). None of those exact morpheme combinations were attested as a real place in the corpus, but the tag-pattern structure they instantiate was attested hundreds of times.

This is the exact scenario the tag-level co-occurrence approach handles well that morpheme-level co-occurrence would have killed:

- Morpheme-level: P(Brait-, -ham) ≈ 0 (never attested as a specific pair). P(Braitham, Gate) = 0. Kills the output.
- Tag-level: P(size, habitative) for word-1 internal compound is high. P(habitative, boundary/infrastructure) for word-2 follow-up is moderate. Both supported by hundreds of attested toponyms (Long-X-Gate, Great-X-Bridge, Broad-X-Cross). The novel combination of specific morphemes within those classes is exactly what we want.

Adding a regression test as part of this ticket's acceptance criteria:

  def test_generator_still_produces_braitham_gate_shaped_names():
      '''Rando produced this; the new architecture must not lose the
      capability for this kind of novel-yet-plausible combination.'''
      samples = [generate() for _ in range(5000)]
      matching = [
          s for s in samples
          if has_pattern(s, words=2,
                         word1_tags=(('size','descriptive'), ('habitative',)),
                         word2_tags=('boundary','infrastructure'))
      ]
      assert len(matching) > 5  # rare but should fire

This is the load-bearing test that prevents the sophisticated probabilistic model from accidentally narrowing the output distribution to only-attested-shapes. The novelty-knob (α/β mixture) needs to stay loose enough that this test passes at the default setting.
close_reason: Closed

title: Norman+English manorial-affix layering as a generation pattern
description:
A specific compositional pattern that English place naming captures densely: English/ON base name + French manorial affix marking the lord's family. Captures the political history of conquest layering directly in the toponym.

Real examples (Domesday and post-Conquest):
- Stoke Mandeville (English Stoke + Norman Mandeville family)
- Ashby de la Zouch (ON Ashby + Norman La Zouche family)
- Newton Poppleford (English Newton + Norman Poppleford family)
- Stanton Lacy (English Stanton + Norman Lacy family)
- Castle Cary (English Castle + Norman Cary family)

As a generation pattern: pick any English/ON base toponym, attach a Norman manorial affix from a sampled noble family. Output reads as 'a town that was conquered and now bears its conqueror's family name' — gameable settlement-name structure encoding political history.

Implementation: needs (a) a corpus of Norman manorial families (extractable from Domesday + later subsidy rolls — many in PD scholarly compilations), (b) a generation mode where a base name is paired with an affix from this corpus.

Killer for fantasy worldbuilding: the GM picks 'this region was conquered 200 years ago by House Mortemer' and the generator produces a region of base names with Mortemer affixes ('Hadenham Mortemer', 'Crowley Mortemer', etc.). Settlement-name pattern explicitly encodes the political history.

title: Selectional restrictions on etymon co-occurrence
description:
Place-name morphemes aren't freely combinable. -by (ON 'farm/settlement') composes with personal names and topographic features but NOT with other settlement generics. -ham and -tūn both 'farm/settlement' but they have different productive periods and pair with different typical first-elements (Ekwall's introduction details this).

Currently the schema lets the generator combine any first-element with any post-element. That'd produce 'Brycgham' (bridge + home), which never occurs in real corpus and reads as wrong even if morphologically possible.

Schema addition: per-etymon tag column or a new selection_restrictions table:
  etymon_selection (
    etymon_id,
    can_compose_with TEXT,  -- 'personal-name', 'topographic', 'patronymic-ing', etc.
    role TEXT               -- 'as-first-element', 'as-second-element'
  )

Generation samples only morpheme pairs whose selection restrictions are compatible.

This can be hand-coded from Ekwall/Mawer's introductions OR learned probabilistically from the corpus (see wyrd-{co-occurrence ticket}).
notes: DEFER — subsumed by wyrd-mj2's tag-level co-occurrence model per the reframe in mj2's notes. The semantic-tag co-occurrence (now populated in every culture's proportions bundle: 391-973 pairs per culture across 22-45 tags) captures most selectional restrictions for free. Revisit only if specific selectional facts persist that tags can't capture (e.g. 'this morpheme only takes patronymics, never personal names' — same tag, different sub-class).

title: Phonological mutation / sandhi as post-composition layer
description:
When the generator assembles a name from morphemes, language-specific phonological rules need to apply at the composition boundary. Without these, output reads as wrong-language to native readers (and even non-native readers parse it as 'artificial' without articulating why).

Languages requiring mutation/sandhi rules at composition time:
- Welsh: soft mutation (Caer + Dyfn → Caerddyfn / Caerddyfnaint or whatever the actual rule produces), nasal mutation, aspirate mutation. Mutation depends on the grammatical relation between the two morphemes (genitive, possessive, modifier).
- Old Irish: lenition, eclipsis. Triggered by similar grammatical contexts.
- French: liaison and elision (le + arbre → l'arbre, Saint + Étienne → Saint-Étienne).
- Old English: i-mutation in some compound formations; assimilation rules at consonant-cluster boundaries.

Architecture: a per-language composition_rule function that takes (left-morpheme, right-morpheme, relation) and produces the surface compound. Stored as a Python module per language (welsh_mutation.py, oldirish_mutation.py, etc.) since the rules are linguistic data, not lexicon data.

Critical for the elven=Welsh, noble=French, common=OE registers to feel right. Without it, generated 'Welsh' names will look obviously synthesized to anyone who knows Welsh.

Pairs with wyrd-q5v (composition patterns) — the patterns specify SHAPE, this specifies the phonological glue between slots.
notes: BLOCKED on wyrd-q5v (per-language composition patterns). Sandhi/mutation needs the composition-pattern layer to know the grammatical relation between morphemes (genitive, possessive, modifier) so the right mutation rule fires. Revisit after wyrd-q5v ships.

title: Regression-prevention: hedged etymology extraction in SYSTEM_PROMPT
description:
Per user direction (this conversation): scholars frequently hedge etymologies ('perhaps from', 'possibly', 'I only make a guess'). The previous SYSTEM_PROMPT instructed the LLM to set found=false for any case where the scholar 'declines.' This conflated two different failure modes:

  (a) Scholar provides NO etymological claim (cross-reference, attestation list, 'meaning unknown')
  (b) Scholar provides a HEDGED etymology

The previous prompt declined on both, losing all the (b) data. Per Skeat alone, 30-50% of declines are likely hedged etymologies we should be capturing.

Updated SYSTEM_PROMPT to distinguish these. Hedged etymologies now extract with confidence='low' and the hedge phrase in notes. Test case verified on Caxton (Skeat: 'I only make a guess when suggesting...'):
- Old prompt: declined (data lost)
- New prompt: extracted 'Cages' as the genitive prefix, conf='low', notes captures the hedge

Regression-prevention test added in test_kenning_llm_extractor.py: test_system_prompt_distinguishes_hedge_from_no_claim. Asserts the prompt contains 'perhaps', 'hedge', confidence=low, 'no etymological claim', and 'still useful'.

FOLLOW-UP work this enables (filed elsewhere):
- wyrd-bgr: extending the review pipeline to re-process Tier 1 declines now that we know many were hedged-etymology false-declines.
- Re-mining: running Mawer/Skeats with the new prompt would recover the ~120-200 hedged toponyms currently in the 'declined' bucket.
close_reason: content already shipped: SYSTEM_PROMPT in llm_extractor.py distinguishes hedge from no-claim (lines 105, 135, 141), and tests/test_kenning_llm_extractor.py:182 test_system_prompt_distinguishes_hedge_from_no_claim asserts the regression-prevention guard. Ticket was filed to track existing-but-tracked work; both halves are present and green.

title: Architectural gap: Tier-2 review never sees Tier-1 declines
description:
Identified during Watson investigation. Current review pipeline has a structural blind spot:

- Tier 1 (Qwen) processes every entry. Output is one of: accepted-with-elements (writes toponym_etymology row), declined (writes only a toponym row, no etymology), rejected (writes nothing).
- Tier 2 (Gemini review) only queries toponym_etymology rows tagged as Qwen-extracted with low/medium confidence.

Result: Qwen-DECLINED entries are never re-examined by Gemini or any later tier. If Qwen wrongly declined (which it demonstrably does — see Watson where it declined 95% of Celtic etymology entries that Haiku extracts cleanly from), that data is permanently lost.

Estimated invisible material based on Watson finding (Qwen 3.4% accept vs Haiku ~22%):
- Mawer: 394 declines × likely 30%+ recoverable = ~120 toponyms with hidden etymology
- Watson 1904: ~362 declines × likely 60%+ recoverable = ~200+ toponyms (the Celtic case is extreme)
- Across all Celtic books we'd mine the same way

PROPOSED FIX: extend lexicon review to support a 'declines' mode that picks up toponyms where:
- A toponym row exists for a book
- Either no toponym_etymology row exists, OR the latest one is low-confidence with no elements
- AND no row tagged with the target review-provider exists

Then layered review naturally catches gaps:
  wyrd kenning lexicon review sources/ --mode declines --provider haiku
  → re-extracts what Qwen missed using a stronger Tier 1 candidate

Quick-validation path before building the architectural fix: run Haiku on 50 of Mawer's Qwen-declined toponyms, measure recovery rate. If Haiku extracts from >30% of those, that confirms the gap is real and motivates the architectural change.

title: Empirical finding: Sonnet doesn't lift over Gemini on etymology mining
description:
Tested Anthropic Sonnet 4.6 as a third-tier review provider on Mawer disagreement cases (where Qwen and Gemini gave different breakdowns). Result: Sonnet added noise rather than signal.

SAMPLE (5 disagreement cases, Mawer Northumberland-Durham):
- Allen: Sonnet matched Gemini (tie)
- Angerton: Sonnet hallucinated +tun post-element (Mawer never compounds it). REJECTED by validator.
- Ardley: Sonnet over-canonicalized 'leak' (Mawer's older spelling) to 'leah'. REJECTED.
- Backworth: Sonnet invented a personal-name compound (bacca+worð) when Mawer explicitly hedges the etymology and says it might be named after a school. REJECTED.
- Bagraw: Sonnet matched Gemini (tie).

Net: 0 wins, 3 losses (validator-rejected hallucinations), 2 ties. Cost: ~5 cents.

Plus: there's no 'Gemini-declined' cohort to test Sonnet's rescue capability on Mawer — Gemini accepted all 98 reviewed entries.

INTERPRETATION: Gemini Flash's 'extract only what the text claims' calibration is BETTER matched to etymology mining than Sonnet's 'smart-extrapolation-beyond-the-text' instinct. For this task, source fidelity > inference quality. Sonnet's strength becomes a liability against a strict form-in-body validator (which is what we want).

DECISION:
- Keep the Anthropic provider code (anthropic_extractor.py, --provider anthropic in CLI). Built, tested, idempotent. Available if calibration thinking changes or for different tasks.
- DO NOT run a Sonnet review pass on existing mined data. Negative ROI.
- Reserve Anthropic API budget for user-facing runtime features (wyrd-e67 Bedrock-style use cases) where smart extrapolation is the bottleneck: 'describe this name's setting', 'translate this homebrew deity', 'generate name variations in the same style'.

Future revisit conditions: if we find a class of entries where Gemini consistently fails (e.g. very obscure Celtic books with non-standard formatting), or if we encounter a corpus with very different characteristics (Mesoamerican, Asian languages), Sonnet may add lift there.
close_reason: finding documented in DECISIONS.md D19 'Sonnet review doesn't lift over Gemini Flash for this task'. The decision (keep anthropic_extractor as a provider option but don't run a Sonnet review pass; reserve budget for runtime user-facing features) is the operating policy already.

title: Body-signal regex too narrow — Celtic / Gaelic books under-yield
description:
The dictionary parser's body-signal validator (added in wyrd-u32) recognizes English-etymology markers (O.E., A.S., O.N., A.F., M.E., year, Phonology) but doesn't include Celtic markers (G., Ir., W., Corn., Brit., Gael.). As a result, Gaelic-language books drop catastrophically:

- Gillies Argyll: 155 → 41 entries
- Johnston Scotland 1892: 2 entries (was higher before)
- Moore Isle of Man: 3 entries (was higher before)

The fix is to broaden _ENTRY_BODY_SIGNALS to include single-letter language abbreviations:
  | G\. | Ir\. | W\. | Corn\. | Brit\. | Gael(?:ic)? | Old\s+Ir(?:ish)? | Welsh

Plus probably: the 'from <foreign-word>' or '<word> = <gloss>' equation patterns common in Celtic etymology books.

Test against Gillies and Watson 1926 to verify the broadened signals catch real Celtic entries without re-introducing the Mawer false-positives that wyrd-u32 fixed.

Lower priority but blocks mining of the Celtic-register sources we'd want for elven/old-folk register densification.
notes:
Related: this also explains why Qwen 9B is declining ~93% of Watson's Ross-and-Cromarty entries (13 accepted out of 240+ at the time of writing). Qwen 9B is English-trained — it sees Watson's Gaelic etymology with G./Ir./W. markers and lacks the English-etymology markers (O.E./A.S.) that anchor its understanding, so it declines.

This makes Watson and other Celtic books exactly the cohort where the layered review (Gemini → Sonnet) might pay off MORE than on English-etymology books like Mawer. Stronger multilingual models would have less English-bias.

Proposed test once Watson Qwen mining finishes: re-mine Watson with --provider gemini (full re-mine, not review), compare accept rate to Qwen's. If Gemini gets >40%, the layered strategy is validated for Celtic corpora and worth running across Joyce, Macbain, Gillies, Watson 1926, etc.
Empirical confirmation in progress: Haiku 4.5 running on Watson 1904 in parallel with Qwen. After 130/380 entries, Haiku has 28 accepted vs Qwen's 13 across the full 380 (final). Haiku's per-entry rate ~22% vs Qwen's 3.4%. ~6× lift from switching Tier 1 from Qwen to Haiku for Celtic content. Total Haiku cost projected at ~$0.50 for the full Watson book.
close_reason: Landed in PR #4: parser body-bounds + Celtic body-signal regex broadened. Joyce/Moore/Johnston yields lifted from 0-3 to 70-1100+ entries each.

title: European place-name mining: all the languages with credible PD sources
description:
Mine the major European language families that have credible pre-1929 toponymic scholarship, treating all as morally-neutral palette options for fantasy worldbuilding. The 'dark/menacing' coding is a SEPARATE orthogonal layer (harsh-phonology + grim-semantic-tag filters) that applies to any language. No language is pre-positioned as the bad-guy register.

Languages with good PD source coverage:
- German: Ernst Förstemann, 'Altdeutsches Namenbuch' (1856-), foundational. August Pott, 'Die Personennamen' (1859). Solid PD.
- Italian: Dante Olivieri, Francesco D'Ovidio — early 1900s
- Iberian (Spanish/Portuguese): Madoz's 'Diccionario geográfico-estadístico-histórico de España' (1845-50, very PD); Leite de Vasconcelos for Portuguese
- Slavic (already filed wyrd-i88): Miklosich, Brückner — see that ticket
- Hungarian / Finnish (Uralic): scrappier PD coverage, Hunfalvy late 1800s
- Basque (pre-IE European): Resurrección María de Azkue's dictionary (early 1900s)
- Romanian: Romance + Slavic + Dacian substrate; some early-1900s scholarship
- Greek (already filed wyrd-tqj): Pape, Smith
- Albanian: very limited
- Celtic, Norse, OE, Norman-French, Latin, Welsh: already in our corpus

Each new register adds a distinct fantasy-worldbuilding option:
- German   → Black Forest / mittelmark / pastoral mountain settings
- Italian  → Renaissance city-states / Mediterranean trade
- Spanish  → Iberian frontier / colonial / Reconquista
- Hungarian → Carpathian / steppe-edge
- Finnish  → frozen north / shamanic
- Basque   → ancient pre-IE mystery (genuinely no relatives — a real ethnolinguistic isolate)
- Romanian → Balkan / Dacian-tinted

None is pre-coded for fantasy role. The orthogonal filters (--harsh, --grim, --pastoral, --noble, --imperial) compose with any of these to produce specific moods.

Mining priority order (estimating yield/effort): German > Italian > Spanish > Hungarian > Basque > others.

title: Slavic register for orcish/underdark/foreign-menacing flavor
description:
Slavic fills a specific niche in fantasy register: 'foreign here-and-now-other' rather than 'lost ancient' (substrate) or 'harsh-mountain' (Norse). Tolkien's Black Speech is Slavic-tinted on purpose; fantasy genre has inherited the Slavic-as-menacing convention via D&D's Drow language and decades of pulp novels.

Distinctive markers (what makes Slavic READ slavic to English ears):
- Consonant clusters English doesn't use: Wrocław, Szczecin, Brzeszcze, mst-, pszcz-, vstr-
- /x/ phoneme (Cyrillic Х, Polish ch, transliterated kh) — harsh, no English equivalent
- Final-syllable stress contrasting with English's penult/initial preference
- Distinctive suffixes: -grad (fortress-city), -gorod, -sk, -ovsk, -yn, -ov/-ev/-ow, -ka

Mythology layer (rich material for underdark/dark-fantasy):
- Veles (god of the underworld and cattle), Nav (the dead), Mokosh, Chernobog
- Folk tales: Koschei the Deathless, Baba Yaga, vodyanoy, leshy, rusalka
- Distinct from Norse-mythological or Celtic-fae figures — a separate dark-magic register

PD source coverage (thinner than British-isles but workable):
- Franz Miklosich, 'Die slavischen Ortsnamen aus Appellativen' (1872-74) — foundational comparative Slavic toponymy
- Aleksander Brückner, Słownik etymologiczny języka polskiego (1927) — barely pre-1929
- Various late-1800s per-country gazetteers (Russian, Czech, Polish)

Suggested language tags:
- slavic-east   (Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian)
- slavic-west   (Polish, Czech, Slovak)
- slavic-south  (Serbian-Croatian, Bulgarian, Macedonian)
- Aggregate parent: slavic-family

Combines with the orcish/darklands register from wyrd-{filed earlier}: --style orcish + --slavic-flavor or --style underdark.

SENSITIVITY: Coding 'Slavic = orc' is a recognizable fantasy convention but it's also Cold War-residue xenophobia. Real Slavic peoples are not orcs. Bundle the data, document the connotations honestly, make Slavic ONE option among several for the dark register (not the default). Same posture as for Indigenous languages in wyrd-668.
notes:
REFRAMED per user: do NOT pre-position Slavic as 'orcish/dark.' Slavic is its own register, equally available for noble/heroic/everyday/menacing — the GM decides at use time, not the engine.

Title rename intent: 'Slavic place-name register for fantasy worldbuilding' (drop the orc/underdark coding).

The 'dark/menacing' effect is a SEPARATE orthogonal layer:
- Phonological skew filter (--harsh): prefer harsh consonant clusters, short syllables, voiced-stop endings — works on ANY language
- Semantic-tag filter (--grim): include only morphemes tagged grim/mortuary/monstrous/battle — works on ANY language

These two filters can apply to Slavic, OE, Latin, Welsh, etc. independently of the language's 'native' register. So a GM gets:
  --style slavic-east --everyday      → ordinary Russian-style village names
  --style slavic-east --harsh --grim  → menacing Russian-style fortress
  --style old-english --harsh --grim  → menacing Saxon-style fortress
  --style norman --everyday           → ordinary Norman village
  --style norman --harsh --grim       → menacing Norman keep

Each combination is legitimate. No language is pre-coded as the bad-guy register.

title: Dutch / Afrikaans register: mercantile-cities + colonial-frontier flavor
description:
Add Dutch and Afrikaans as fantasy registers for niches the British-isles palette doesn't cover well: mercantile city-states (Hanseatic-fantasy, Waterdeep-style canal cities), low-country wetlands, and colonial-frontier settings.

NOT a major densifier for existing British-isles consensus — Dutch's direct impact on English place naming is small (East Anglia fenland settlements, William III's nobility post-1689). The richer toponymic veins are in former Dutch-colonized regions: New Netherland (NY/NJ), South Africa (Afrikaans), Suriname.

Distinctive markers that read as Dutch to English ears:
- Suffixes: -dam, -haven, -poort, -werp, -dijk, -meer, -laan, -burgh
- Afrikaans suffixes: -fontein, -bosch, -veld, -kraal, -stad, -berg
- Phonemes: oe (/uː/), ij (/ɛi/), ui (/œy/), sch- (/sx/), throat-g (/ɣ/), doubled-vowel length

Fantasy register payoffs:
- 'Hanseatic merchant city-state' setting (think a Tolkien-ier version of D&D's Sword Coast): canal cities, trade leagues, merchant princes. Dutch is THE language for this.
- 'Trekker frontier' setting: Afrikaans-flavored. Hard land, settler outposts, distinctive from European-noble or English-pastoral. -fontein and -berg-driven.
- 'Low-country wetlands' with rich water-management vocabulary (polder, sluis, boezem, dijk, waard).

PD source coverage:
- Dutch proper: Johan Winkler (1837-1916), Verwijs & Verdam Middelnederlandsch Woordenboek (late 1800s), G.J. Boekenoogen dialectology (early 1900s)
- Afrikaans: sparser PD coverage, most compilations are mid-20th-c. Could lean on Dutch sources + a small set of distinctive Afrikaans markers seeded by hand.
- New Netherland (NY) toponymy: various NY historical society publications, late-1800s, PD

Language tags: 'dutch' (proper), 'afrikaans' (post-Cape derivation, where distinct).

Lower priority than the British-isles densification work since the consensus uplift is small, but a useful future register for fantasy worldbuilding diversity.

title: Mining: Nahuatl place-name corpus (separate from Mayan)
description:
Nahuatl is Uto-Aztecan, completely separate from Mayan. Different phonology, different morphology, different fantasy feel.

Distinctive Nahuatl markers:
- -tl lateral affricate suffix (Tenochtitlan, Tlaxcala, Cuauhnahuac, Quetzalcoatl) — iconic and untranslatable
- -tzin / -tzintli reverential
- Hu- representing /w/ (Huitzilopochtli, Cuauhtemoc, Tehuacán)
- -co / -tlan locative suffixes (Mexico = 'place of the Mexica')
- X = /ʃ/ (Xochimilco, Xochicalco — shared with Mayan orthographically only)
- 'Coatl' (serpent), 'tepec' (hill), 'mil' (cornfield), 'atl' (water) — high-frequency morphemes

PD sources to mine:
- Frederick Starr, 'Aztec Place-Names' (1920) — already found in our archive.org search
- Cecilio Robelo, 'Toponimia mexicana' (late 1800s)
